1.1.note: 70 questions in 120 minutes: 60 scored, 10 unscored. Every question is a scenario. Applies to exams taken on or after December 7, 2026.

questions.stem: A property insurer asks you to 'let Claude handle claims end to end.' Claims arrive as PDFs (police reports, repair estimates, photos). Payouts are governed by policy rules already encoded in the insurer's claims system of record, and regulators require a licensed adjuster to sign off on any payout above $10,000. Which division of work is the most defensible architecture?
options: Claude extracts and normalizes facts from the documents and flags inconsistencies between them; the claims system of record computes the payout; a licensed adjuster approves anything above $10,000 using Claude's summary.
An orchestrator coordinates extraction, rules, fraud and payment agents on the most capable model, approving a payout only when all four agents independently agree on the amount.
A Claude agent reads the documents and computes payouts from policy rules in its system prompt, auto-paying claims under $10,000 and escalating larger ones to an adjuster with a full rationale.
Fine-tune a model on several years of historical claims so it predicts payouts directly, with an adjuster reviewing a statistically sized sample each week for quality assurance.
questions.explanation: Decompose by who is reliable at what. Claude is strong at reading messy multimodal documents and spotting inconsistencies; deterministic payout math already lives in the system of record and should stay there; the regulatory sign-off is a human task. Putting rules in a prompt (C) makes money movement depend on probabilistic recall of rules. More agents (B) add cost and failure points without adding a capability the problem needs. Any sampling scheme (D) violates the explicit sign-off requirement for every payout above $10,000.

questions.stem: A finance team runs a monthly reconciliation: pull ledger exports, match transactions against bank statements, classify the unmatched items into one of eight known exception types, and draft a variance memo. The steps and their order never change; only the data does. The team wants it to be auditable and cheap. Which solution form fits best?
options: An autonomous agent with tools for the ledger, bank feeds and memo system, allowed to decide which steps to run and in which order so it can adapt to each month's data.
A single long-context call containing the full ledger export and bank statements, with structured output, asked to reconcile, classify exceptions and write the memo in one pass.
Orchestrator-workers: one worker per account reconciles in parallel, and the orchestrator merges results and drafts the memo, which shortens wall-clock time at month end.
A code-defined workflow: deterministic matching in code, Claude only for exception classification (structured output) and memo drafting, with validation gates.
questions.explanation: When the path is known in advance, a workflow beats an agent: it is cheaper, predictable and auditable, and code handles the exact matching that a model would only approximate. Agents earn their cost when the sequence of steps cannot be predicted. Dumping all data into one call (B) asks the model to do exact arithmetic over thousands of rows. Orchestrator-workers (C) is for dynamic decomposition; here the decomposition is fixed and known. An autonomous agent (A) would choose its own steps for a process whose steps are already known, adding cost and unpredictability to work that needs an audit trail.

questions.stem: You are deciding between a code-defined workflow and an autonomous agent for a new capability. Which TWO characteristics of the task are the strongest signals that an agent is justified?
options: The task must complete with very low, predictable latency, so the system should adapt its steps dynamically to avoid unnecessary work on simple inputs.
The task is open-ended so a fixed path would miss cases, and the environment gives feedback (tool results, test outcomes) the model can act on.
Every action must follow a strict sequence mandated by regulators, so a model that reasons about each step is needed to ensure compliance at every point.
The number and order of steps depend on what earlier tool results reveal and cannot be enumerated in advance.
Request volume is very high, so an autonomous system is needed to keep up without growing the operations team proportionally.
questions.explanation: Agents fit problems where the path is unpredictable and the model can use environmental feedback to choose the next step. Low, predictable latency (A) and strict mandated sequences (C) favor workflows, which have fixed, bounded steps. High volume (E) argues for automation in general, not for an agent specifically; a workflow or single call automates high volume more cheaply.

questions.stem: A research assistant uses an orchestrator that spawns five subagents to investigate subtopics. Each subagent returns the full text of every page it read. After a few runs the orchestrator hits context limits and its final synthesis quality drops. What is the best fix?
options: Enable tool-result clearing in each subagent with a low trigger threshold, so their contexts stay small and the volume of text they produce shrinks accordingly.
Reduce the number of subagents to two broader ones, so less overlapping text comes back and the orchestrator has fewer documents to reconcile during synthesis.
Have each subagent return a condensed, structured finding (key claims plus source references), and write full source material to external storage the orchestrator can fetch if needed.
Move the orchestrator to the model with the largest available context window, so all subagent output fits and nothing the subagents found is lost before synthesis.
questions.explanation: A key benefit of subagents is context isolation: they do the heavy reading and return a distilled result. Returning raw pages defeats that. Structured summaries with references keep the orchestrator focused while preserving traceability. A larger window (D) postpones the problem and dilutes attention. Fewer subagents (B) reduces coverage. Clearing inside the subagents (A) does not change what they send back to the orchestrator.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to migrate a large codebase from one logging library to another. Which files need changes, and how each must change, is only known after analysing call sites; some files need trivial edits and others need refactors. Which pattern best fits?
options: Routing: a classifier labels each file as edit or skip, and every file labeled edit goes to a single specialized migration prompt tuned on examples.
Orchestrator-workers: an orchestrator analyses the codebase, decides which subtasks exist and delegates them with tailored instructions, then integrates and verifies.
Parallelization (sectioning): split the repository into equal folders and process each folder with the same migration prompt simultaneously to minimize total runtime.
Prompt chaining: a fixed chain of analyse, edit and test steps applied to the whole repository, with a validation gate after each step before continuing.
questions.explanation: Orchestrator-workers fits when the subtasks cannot be predefined and depend on the input; the orchestrator decides them dynamically. Sectioning (C) works when subtasks are known and independent, but equal folder splits ignore the very different work each file needs. A fixed chain over the whole repo (D) will not fit in context or adapt per file. Routing (A) helps triage but provides no mechanism for tailored refactors and integration.

questions.stem: A CFO states the goal for a support assistant: 'Reduce cost per resolved ticket by 30% without lowering CSAT.' Which TWO design decisions most directly align the architecture to this business goal?
options: Maximize the share of tickets the AI closes, since every ticket closed without a human directly reduces cost per resolved ticket.
Use the most capable model for every request so quality holds steady; the savings come from deflecting more tickets away from human agents.
Add specialist agents per ticket category so each category gets expert handling, raising resolution quality enough to offset the extra model calls.
Establish a baseline for cost per resolved ticket and CSAT before launch, and instrument both so they can be reported by ticket category.
Route by difficulty: a cheap model takes simple intents, a larger model takes complex ones, with defined human escalation.
questions.explanation: The goal is a ratio (cost per resolved ticket) with a constraint (CSAT). You cannot claim a 30% reduction without a baseline and per-category measurement, and tiered routing attacks cost while protecting quality where it matters. Using the largest model everywhere (B) inflates cost. Optimizing raw closure rate (A) counts tickets that reopen as resolved and can tank CSAT. More agents (C) adds cost and latency without a stated benefit.

questions.stem: Users ask an HR assistant two kinds of questions: 'How is PTO accrued for part-time staff?' and 'How many PTO days do I have left?' The current design answers both from a RAG index built from a nightly export of policies and HRIS data. Complaints mention wrong balances. What is the best architectural change?
options: Increase top-k and add a reranker for balance questions, so the correct employee's record is reliably retrieved even when many records look similar.
Apply contextual retrieval so each balance chunk is prefixed with the employee's name and department, making the right record far more likely to be retrieved.
Increase the HRIS export frequency from nightly to hourly, so balance chunks in the index are at most an hour old and policy and balance answers share one pipeline.
Keep RAG for policy questions, and add a tool that queries the HRIS live for the authenticated employee's current PTO balance.
questions.explanation: Retrieval is the wrong mechanism for data that must be current and is specific to one user. Balances are live state: query the system of record through a tool, scoped to the authenticated user. More frequent exports (C) still serve stale data and put personal data into a shared index. Contextual retrieval (B) and larger top-k (A) improve finding chunks, not their freshness, and they raise the risk of exposing other employees' records.

questions.stem: A customer-service agent escalates to a human when it cannot resolve an issue. Human agents complain they must re-read the whole transcript and often re-ask the customer for details. What is the most effective design change?
options: Give human agents access to the agent's full reasoning and tool trace, so they can see exactly what it did and why at each step.
On escalation, have the agent attach a structured handoff to the ticket: customer, issue, what was tried, tool results and open questions.
Have the agent summarize the issue back to the customer and ask them to confirm it with the human agent, so nothing is misunderstood.
Escalate earlier in the conversation so transcripts are shorter and humans can read the full history quickly before responding.
questions.explanation: Handoffs are an architectural interface. A structured summary that carries forward verified facts and attempted actions lets the human continue rather than restart. Escalating earlier (D) increases human load without fixing the handoff. A full reasoning and tool trace (A) gives the human even more to read than the transcript. Having the customer re-confirm the issue with the human (C) still makes them repeat themselves, which is the failure being reported.

questions.stem: A localization team translates marketing copy into 12 languages. Brand guidelines define clear, checkable criteria (tone, banned terms, length limits, keeping product names untranslated). First drafts often violate one criterion. Which pattern best fits?
options: Raise the temperature and add the brand guidelines to the prompt, so the model explores more phrasings and is more likely to land on a compliant one.
Generate ten drafts in parallel per language and use a second call to pick the one that best matches the brand voice overall.
Evaluator-optimizer: a second call checks each draft against the criteria and feeds back fixes, with an iteration cap.
An autonomous agent with web browsing that researches each market's conventions before writing, so drafts reflect local norms as well as brand rules.
questions.explanation: Evaluator-optimizer works when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement measurably helps, which matches checkable brand rules. Cap iterations to bound cost and latency, and enforce hard rules such as banned terms and length limits in code where possible. Higher temperature (A) increases variability, not compliance. Market research (D) addresses a different problem. Picking a draft by overall voice (B) neither checks each criterion nor fixes the violations.

questions.stem: A chat assistant has a p95 latency of 6.5 s. The pipeline runs sequentially: an input-policy classifier, query rewriting, hybrid retrieval with reranking of 150 candidates, and a final answer from a large model with no streaming. The SLA is 'first visible text within 2 s at p95.' Which TWO changes most directly address the SLA without weakening safety?
options: Remove the policy classifier from the request path and run it asynchronously on logs afterwards, flagging violations for review the next morning.
Stream the answer, and run the policy classifier in parallel with retrieval and generation, gating release of streamed text on its result.
Raise max_tokens so answers complete in a single call, avoiding continuation requests that add round-trips under load.
Report average latency rather than p95 in the SLA, since averages better reflect the typical user's experience across the day.
Rerank fewer candidates (e.g. 50) or use a smaller reranker, after confirming retrieval recall stays acceptable.
questions.explanation: The SLA measures time to first visible text, so streaming plus parallelising the guardrail removes the sequential classifier delay, as long as release is gated on its verdict. Reranking cost scales with candidate count, and it can be tuned while monitoring recall. Removing the classifier (A) weakens safety. Changing the metric (D) hides the problem. max_tokens (C) caps output length; it does not reduce latency to first token.

questions.stem: A commercial lender's COO asks for 'an AI that replaces our underwriters.' Underwriters spend about 60% of their time gathering and summarizing financials from borrower documents and 40% making credit judgments that carry regulatory accountability. What should your proposed solution scope be?
options: An agent that makes credit decisions end to end, with underwriters auditing a risk-weighted sample afterwards and able to reverse any decision within 48 hours.
A policy Q&A assistant that underwriters can consult about lending guidelines, reducing the time they spend searching internal documentation.
Claude drafts a standardized credit memo with citations to source pages; underwriters make and own the credit decision; success is time-to-decision and memo accuracy.
Decline the engagement, because credit decisions carry regulatory accountability that cannot be shared with an AI system under any architecture.
questions.explanation: Good solution design starts with scoping who does what. The highest-value, lowest-risk work is the 60% spent gathering and summarizing, which Claude does well. The accountable judgment stays with humans, and citations make the draft verifiable. Full automation (A) conflicts with regulatory accountability. Declining (D) ignores a large, safe value pool. A policy chatbot (B) misses where the time actually goes.

questions.stem: A tax-preparation assistant must compute estimated quarterly payments from figures the user provides, then explain the result. Early tests show occasional arithmetic errors in multi-step calculations. Which design is most appropriate?
options: Enable extended thinking with a generous budget, so the model works through each calculation step by step and checks its own arithmetic before answering.
Expose a deterministic calculation tool or code execution; Claude gathers the inputs, calls the tool, and explains the tool's result to the user.
Add few-shot examples of correct multi-step calculations to the prompt, covering each income type, so the model follows the demonstrated procedure.
Have the model compute the result twice independently and reconcile any difference before answering, which catches most arithmetic slips.
questions.explanation: Deterministic computation belongs in code. Claude is excellent at collecting inputs, deciding what to compute and explaining results, but exact multi-step arithmetic should be delegated to a tool. Thinking (A) and examples (C) reduce errors without guaranteeing correctness. Computing twice (D) does not catch an error both attempts share and still guarantees nothing.

questions.stem: In a multi-agent system, an orchestrator delegates 'research competitor pricing' to three subagents. Results overlap heavily, two subagents researched the same competitors, and one returned free-form essays the orchestrator struggled to merge. What is the root cause most worth fixing?
options: Subagents each have isolated contexts; giving them a single shared context would let them coordinate and divide the work themselves.
The subagents run on a smaller model than the orchestrator, so they lack the judgment to divide the work sensibly among themselves.
Subagents run in parallel, so they cannot see each other's progress; running them sequentially would let each one avoid repeating earlier work.
The delegation lacks explicit boundaries: each subagent needs a distinct objective, a non-overlapping scope, an expected output format, and what not to do.
questions.explanation: Vague delegation causes duplicated effort and unmergeable outputs. A good task description gives each worker a clear objective, non-overlapping scope, an output schema and boundaries. A model upgrade (B) does not fix ambiguous instructions. Running sequentially (C) removes the parallelism benefit. Sharing one context (A) removes the isolation that makes subagents useful.

questions.stem: A coding agent delegates 'find all places where we read user PII' to a subagent. The subagent returns a list that includes test fixtures and ignores the team's definition of PII, which was discussed in the main conversation earlier. What explains this, and what is the fix?
options: The subagent ran out of context while scanning the repository; enable compaction so it can retain the definitions as it works.
The parent should have used plan mode before delegating, so the subagent would receive the approved plan and follow it.
The subagent uses a less capable model than the parent; switch it to the same model so it applies the same understanding of PII.
Subagents start from a fresh context, so the delegation prompt must restate the team's definitions and constraints.
questions.explanation: A subagent works in an isolated context. Anything it needs, such as the team's PII definition and the instruction to exclude test fixtures, must be passed in the task description. Changing models (C) or enabling compaction (A) does not supply missing information. Plan mode (B) is unrelated to what the subagent sees.

questions.stem: A ticketing agent calls create_ticket(subject, body). After network timeouts, the agent loop retries, and support sees duplicate tickets for the same customer issue. Where should the fix primarily live?
options: Remove retries from the agent loop, surfacing each timeout to the user so they can decide whether to try again.
In the tool: derive an idempotency key from stable business identifiers, check it before creating, and return the existing ticket on repeats.
In the system prompt and tool description: state clearly that the same ticket must not be created twice and that the agent must search for an existing ticket before creating one.
Lower the temperature to 0 so the agent's decisions are deterministic and it does not repeat a tool call it has already made.
questions.explanation: Duplicate side effects must be prevented where the side effect happens. A business-key idempotency check (ideally backed by a unique constraint) makes retries safe whether they come from the loop, the model or the network. Prompt instructions (C) and temperature (D) do not control retries by infrastructure. Removing retries (A) turns transient failures into lost work.

questions.stem: A logistics company receives about 40,000 inbound emails a day that must be sorted into 12 queues. Each email is independent, the categories are stable, and the routing decision feeds a deterministic downstream system. Which solution form is most appropriate?
options: Three agents classify each email independently and vote, which reduces individual errors and gives a natural confidence signal from agreement.
One call per email on a small, fast model, with contrasting examples for confusable queues, structured output limited to the 12 queues, and a human queue.
An agent per email with CRM tools, so it can look up customer history before deciding, improving accuracy on ambiguous emails.
A vector index of past emails, routing each new email to the queue of its most similar historical email, which needs no prompt engineering.
questions.explanation: A high-volume, stable, single-decision classification is the textbook case for one augmented call: cheap, fast and measurable with per-class metrics. Structured output guarantees a valid label, and examples target the confusable pairs. Agents (C) and debates (A) multiply cost and latency for no added capability. Nearest-neighbor lookup (D) inherits historical mislabels and handles novel emails poorly.

questions.stem: A media company needs summaries of about 2 million archived articles for a new search feature launching in six weeks. Every request shares an identical 3,000-token instruction block. Nobody is waiting on any individual summary, and the content is public. Which processing design minimizes cost while meeting the timeline?
options: Message Batches API with the shared instructions first and cached (1-hour TTL), matching results by custom_id and resubmitting failures.
One agent per article category running continuously, so each agent specializes in its category's style and the summaries stay consistent.
Real-time Messages API calls at maximum concurrency with prompt caching on the instruction block, finishing well within the six weeks.
Pack as many articles as fit into each request with the instructions once, cutting per-request overhead and total request count dramatically.
questions.explanation: Non-urgent bulk work fits the Batches API (half price, results within 24 hours). Caching the identical prefix further discounts input, and the 1-hour TTL suits batch timing. Results arrive in any order, so match on custom_id and resubmit errored or expired items. Real-time calls (C) forgo the 50% batch discount. Packing many articles into one request (D) mixes content and makes failures expensive. Category agents (B) add nothing.

questions.stem: Same workload as a nightly bulk summarization job, but the documents are clinical notes containing PHI, and the client uses Anthropic's HIPAA-ready API organization under a BAA. The original design used the Message Batches API for the discount. What should you change?
options: Keep the Batches API; batching is an asynchronous form of the Messages API, so it falls under the same BAA coverage as standard calls.
Run the batch on a plan tier that bundles batch processing with business features, then delete results immediately after downloading them.
Move to standard Messages API calls through a concurrency-controlled queue, keep prompt caching, and verify every feature is BAA-eligible.
Remove patient names and record numbers from the notes before batching, which takes the data outside HIPAA so the batch discount can be kept.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's BAA coverage is feature-specific, and the Batch API is listed as not covered and not accessible for HIPAA-ready API users, while the Messages API and prompt caching are covered. A queue with controlled concurrency gives you throughput without batches. Assuming coverage (A) is the trap; a HIPAA-enabled org rejects non-eligible features with a 400 error. Removing names and record numbers (D) does not meet HIPAA de-identification standards for free-text notes. Using another plan tier (B) is not a covered configuration, and deleting results afterwards does not change that.

questions.stem: An agent performs a data-migration task that runs for several hours, across many context windows, with occasional infrastructure restarts. Which TWO design choices most improve its ability to finish correctly?
options: Make each migration step idempotent, so replaying a step after a restart or timeout does not corrupt or duplicate data.
Have the agent re-plan from scratch after each restart, since a fresh plan adapts to whatever state the data is now in.
Have the model report its confidence after each step and pause the migration for review whenever confidence falls below 80%.
Persist progress outside the conversation (progress file, checkpoints, commits) so a new session can resume.
Keep everything in one continuous conversation on the largest available context window, so the agent keeps every earlier decision in view.
questions.explanation: Long-running agents need externalized state and safe replay. Progress files or checkpoints let a new context pick up where the last one ended, and idempotent steps make restarts harmless. A single growing conversation (E) eventually overflows and degrades. Re-planning from scratch after each restart (B) discards verified progress and risks repeating side effects. Self-reported confidence (C) is poorly calibrated and is not a reliable control.

questions.stem: A legal team wants Claude to review vendor contracts against a 40-point playbook. Outputs will be reviewed by counsel and tracked in a matter-management system. Which TWO output design choices are most important?
options: A narrative memo organized by risk theme, which counsel find easier to read than item lists and which summarizes the overall position.
Structured findings per playbook item (status, risk level, deviation) validated against a schema, so they can be stored and filtered.
Each finding cites the exact contract clauses it relies on, so counsel can verify quickly.
Let the model choose the output format per contract, since some contracts suit tables and others suit prose.
An overall approve or reject recommendation with a confidence score, so counsel can prioritize which contracts to read in full.
questions.explanation: Design the output for its consumers. Structured, schema-valid findings integrate with the matter system and enable tracking, and clause-level citations make human review fast and auditable. Unstructured narrative (A) cannot be tracked per item. A single verdict (E) hides the reasoning counsel must check. Leaving format to the model (D) breaks downstream integration.

questions.stem: A support agent is supposed to escalate when it cannot safely resolve an issue. The current design asks the model to rate its own confidence from 1 to 10 and escalates below 6. Escalation quality is poor: confidently wrong answers are not escalated. What is the better design?
options: Define explicit, checkable escalation triggers from business policy and evaluate them in code or structured fields.
Raise the threshold so the agent escalates below 8, which increases sensitivity and catches more of the confidently wrong answers.
Ask the model to explain its reasoning before scoring its confidence, which grounds the score and improves calibration.
Move to a more capable model, whose confidence scores are better calibrated, so the existing threshold becomes reliable.
questions.explanation: Self-reported confidence is not reliably calibrated, so it cannot be the main escalation control. Escalation should follow explicit business criteria that can be checked. Moving the threshold (B), upgrading the model (D) or asking for justification (C) still rely on the unreliable signal.

questions.stem: An enterprise assistant exposes 70 tools across CRM, billing, HR and IT. Claude increasingly picks the wrong tool, and every request pays for all 70 tool definitions. Which TWO approaches address both problems?
options: Use tool search with defer_loading for rarely used tools, keeping the handful of most-used tools always loaded.
Repeat the full tool documentation in the system prompt, so the model has richer descriptions to choose from on every request.
Prefix tool names by system (crm_, billing_, hr_, it_) and sort them so related tools appear together in the list.
Split work across specialized domain subagents, each holding only the tools for its own domain, behind a router that selects the subagent.
Raise the temperature slightly so the model considers a wider range of tools instead of defaulting to familiar ones.
questions.explanation: Tool-selection accuracy degrades with large tool sets, and every loaded definition costs tokens. Deferred loading through tool search brings in only relevant tools, and domain subagents shrink each agent's tool set while also enforcing least privilege. Duplicating descriptions (B) adds tokens and confusion. Temperature (E) and sorting names (C) do not address either problem.

questions.stem: After launch, users can mark assistant answers with a thumbs-down and a comment. The product owner proposes automatically fine-tuning the model on thumbs-down cases every week. What is the better feedback-loop design?
options: Adopt weekly fine-tuning on thumbs-down cases with the users' comments as corrections, so the model continuously learns from real failures.
Count thumbs-down rates per topic and lower the temperature for topics with the most complaints, making those answers more conservative.
Triage negative feedback by root cause, add representative cases with corrected outcomes to the eval set, fix the cause, and verify against the regression set.
Show recent thumbs-down examples to the model at runtime as examples of what to avoid, so it adapts immediately.
questions.explanation: Feedback should drive diagnosis and evaluation, not blind training. Many failures come from retrieval, prompts or missing data, which fine-tuning will not fix, and some thumbs-downs mark correct but unwelcome answers. Turning failures into eval cases makes improvements measurable and prevents regressions. Automated fine-tuning (A) can bake in noise. Runtime few-shot with bad examples (D) can teach the wrong behavior. Lowering the temperature for complained-about topics (B) treats a symptom without finding the cause, and it doesn't fix wrong facts or missing data.

questions.stem: A product team describes the desired system: 'Users ask questions; the bot answers.' You are documenting the end-to-end design. Which element is most often missing from this kind of description and is essential for a production design?
options: The hosting region and instance sizes, which determine baseline latency and the cost envelope for the service.
The user-interface design, which determines how users phrase their questions and therefore what the model receives.
The choice of programming language and framework, which determines the available SDKs and how the system will be maintained.
The feedback loop: how outputs are logged, evaluated, reviewed and fed back into prompts and evals after launch.
questions.explanation: An end-to-end design covers input, processing, output and feedback. Teams usually specify the first three and forget the loop that lets them measure quality, catch drift and improve safely. Without it there is no evidence the system meets its goals after launch. Hosting sizes (A), the user-interface design (B) and the language or framework (C) are implementation or presentation details that teams rarely forget.

questions.stem: A production outage has three competing theories: a bad deploy, a database lock, and an expired certificate. You want three Claude Code workers to investigate in parallel and to challenge each other's findings as they go, not just report back separately at the end. Which setup fits?
options: Subagents, one per theory, each reporting its conclusion back to the main session when it finishes.
An agent team, where the teammates share a task list and message each other directly as they work.
A single session that works through the three theories one after another and then compares them.
A dynamic workflow that runs one agent per log file and merges all the findings in a script.
questions.explanation: Agent teams let teammates message each other directly and challenge each other's conclusions while they work, which is exactly what competing-hypothesis debugging needs (B). Subagents only report back to the main session, so they can't debate each other (A). A single session loses the parallelism (C). A dynamic workflow runs isolated agents under a fixed script, and those agents don't talk to each other (D).

questions.stem: A team must check 600 API route files for a missing authorization check, then double-check every finding before it goes into a report. The same check applies to every file. Which approach fits best?
options: An agent team of five teammates who split up the files and talk through their results with each other.
A single session that reads all 600 files into one long context and then lists the problems it finds.
A dynamic workflow that runs one agent per file, then a separate verification pass on each finding.
One subagent that reviews all 600 files on its own and returns a short summary of the problems.
questions.explanation: This is the same check repeated many times in parallel, with verification built in, which is what dynamic workflows are for: a script fans out one agent per file and then verifies each finding (C). An agent team suits a few workers who need to debate, not hundreds of identical checks, and costs more (A). One long context or one subagent would overload a single context window and miss files (B, D).

questions.stem: An orchestrator sends 100 documents to subagents. Each subagent returns a verdict, a synthesis step adds up the verdicts it received, and then every flagged document is archived automatically. Some subagents occasionally time out and return nothing. Which TWO changes fix the most serious defects?
options: Have the synthesis step compare the verdicts it received against the 100 inputs and report any that are missing.
Require human approval, or use a reversible soft-archive, before any document is actually archived.
Switch the synthesis step to a larger model so it summarizes the returned verdicts more accurately.
Double the number of subagents so each one handles fewer documents and finishes sooner.
Remove the shared trace ID from the subagent calls to cut down on logging overhead.
questions.explanation: Today a timed-out subagent silently disappears, and the report still looks complete. Comparing results against the input list makes the gaps visible (A). Archiving is irreversible and happens automatically on possibly incomplete data, so it needs a human gate or a reversible version (B). A bigger model doesn't notice missing inputs (C), more subagents don't fix silent failures (D), and the trace ID is good practice that helps debugging (E).

questions.stem: A consulting firm wants an assistant that answers questions about its own proprietary methodologies. These methodologies were never published, so they are not in the model's training data. Which AI property is the main constraint, and what is the standard mitigation?
options: Steerability: write a longer system prompt that describes each methodology in general terms.
Knowledge: retrieve the relevant methodology documents into the context at the time of each question.
Working memory: switch to a model with a larger context window so it remembers more of the firm's work.
Next token prediction: lower the temperature so the model guesses less when it answers questions about methods.
questions.explanation: The model can't know content it was never trained on, which is a knowledge limit. The fix is to supply that content at question time through retrieval (B). A general description in the prompt is too thin and can't cover detailed questions (A). A bigger context window doesn't create knowledge the model never had (C). Lowering temperature doesn't add missing facts (D).

questions.stem: A knowledge assistant will draw on 12,000 reports, each 5 to 80 pages long. The longest report is about 30,000 tokens. Which statement best describes the working-memory constraint?
options: Individual reports are too long for the context window, so each one must be summarized before use.
There is no real constraint, because current context windows can hold the entire collection at once.
Any single report fits easily, but the whole collection far exceeds any context window, so retrieval is needed.
The constraint is output length, because answers about long reports will exceed the model's maximum output tokens.
questions.explanation: A 30,000-token report fits comfortably in a modern context window, so single documents are not the problem (A). The collection as a whole runs to hundreds of millions of tokens, far beyond any context window (B), and that corpus scale is what makes retrieval necessary (C). Output length is unrelated to how much material the system draws on (D).

questions.stem: When retrieval fails to find the right document, an internal assistant still gives a confident, detailed answer that includes project names that sound real but don't exist. Which two AI properties are interacting, and what is the most direct fix?
options: Working memory and steerability: repeat the instructions at the end of every long conversation.
Next token prediction and knowledge: require answers to cite retrieved sources and allow 'not found.'
Steerability and knowledge: fine-tune the model on the firm's project names every quarter.
Next token prediction and working memory: use a larger context window so more documents fit.
questions.explanation: The model writes what sounds plausible (next token prediction) about facts it doesn't have (knowledge), which produces confident invented details. Requiring citations to retrieved sources, and explicitly allowing 'not found,' removes the pressure to fill the gap (B). Repeating instructions targets drift in long conversations, a different problem (A). Fine-tuning doesn't stop invention when retrieval misses (C), and a bigger window doesn't help when the right document was never retrieved (D).

questions.stem: A 30-person strategy team wants to ask questions across about 40 internal reports and draft memos from them. They need no integration with other systems, and they want to start this month. What is the best fit?
options: A custom RAG application with a vector database, an ingestion pipeline and its own chat interface.
A shared project in the team's Claude workspace, with the reports added as project knowledge.
A fine-tuned model trained on the 40 reports, so the team can ask questions without documents.
An autonomous agent that monitors the reports folder and writes new memos every week.
questions.explanation: A small team, a modest document set, no integrations and a fast start point to an off-the-shelf solution: a shared Claude project with the reports as knowledge (B). A custom application takes months and needs maintenance with no added benefit here (A). Fine-tuning isn't the way to add document knowledge (C). An unsupervised weekly agent isn't what was asked for (D).

questions.stem: A single prompt translates a 30-page technical manual, summarizes each chapter, and formats the result for the website. Errors in the translation show up in the summaries, and nobody can tell which step failed. What design helps most?
options: Use one longer, more detailed prompt that explains each of the three tasks more carefully.
Split it into a chain (translate, check, summarize, format) with a check between steps.
Run the single prompt three times and keep whichever output is the longest.
Switch to a larger model, since bigger models handle multi-step tasks without breaking them up.
questions.explanation: Prompt chaining breaks the job into steps that each do one thing, with a check in between, such as terminology checks on the translation. That makes errors easier to catch and to trace to a step (B). A longer single prompt still mixes the steps together (A). Picking the longest output isn't a quality check (C). A bigger model may make fewer errors but still gives no visibility into which step failed (D).

questions.stem: A pharmacy chain's assistant must keep answering basic refill-status questions even when the Claude API is slow or briefly unavailable. Which TWO design choices help most?
options: Answer refill status from the pharmacy system directly when the model is unavailable, with a simple template.
Set a timeout with retries and backoff, and route to a backup region or platform if the primary keeps failing.
Retry the same request every 100 ms without limit, until the API responds successfully.
Cache one generic AI answer and show it for every question while the API is unavailable.
Show an error page and ask users to try again later, since the assistant can't work without the model.
questions.explanation: Simple, critical lookups shouldn't depend on the model: a template fallback keeps refill status working (A). Timeouts with backoff, plus a backup region or platform, handle slowdowns and outages (B). Retrying without limit makes overload worse (C). One generic answer for every question misleads users (D). An error page fails the requirement (E).

questions.stem: A classifier flags suspicious insurance claims for investigation. Missing a fraudulent claim is costly, and a wrong flag only costs an investigator 10 minutes. The team considers running the classifier three times on each claim. How should the results be combined?
options: Flag the claim only when all three runs agree that it is suspicious, so that investigators see as few false flags as possible.
Flag when any one of the three runs says the claim is suspicious, since misses cost more than false flags.
Average the three runs' wording and flag the claim if the average sounds suspicious.
Use only the first run, since a model with temperature 0 gives the same answer on the other two runs anyway.
questions.explanation: How you combine votes should follow the cost of each kind of error. When misses are expensive and false flags are cheap, flag on any single 'suspicious' vote to raise recall (B). Requiring all three to agree does the opposite, cutting false flags at the cost of more misses (A). 'Averaging wording' isn't a real method (C). Runs can differ, which is why voting helps (D).

questions.stem: A marketing team uses a generator-reviewer loop: one prompt writes ad copy, another checks it against 8 brand rules and sends feedback. Sometimes the loop runs 30 rounds and never finishes. What design fix matters most?
options: Remove the reviewer, since a single well-written prompt should get the copy right the first time.
Stop when all 8 rules pass or after a set number of rounds, then send the best draft to a person.
Let the reviewer rewrite the copy itself instead of sending feedback, so fewer rounds are needed.
Switch the reviewer to a stricter model, so that its feedback is clearer and the loop ends sooner.
questions.explanation: An evaluator-optimizer loop needs a clear finish line (all rules pass) and a hard limit on rounds, with a person handling what's still failing (B). Removing the reviewer loses the quality check (A). If the reviewer rewrites the copy, no one checks the rewrite (C). A stricter reviewer can make the loop run even longer (D).

questions.stem: A support system handles 50,000 questions a day. About 85% are simple lookups, and 15% need careful multi-step reasoning. Using the most capable model for everything is over budget. What design fits?
options: Use the cheapest model for everything, and accept lower quality on the hard questions.
Route each question with a fast classifier: simple ones to a small model, hard ones to a larger model.
Ask users to tick a box saying whether their question is simple or complex before they submit it to the assistant.
Send every question to both models and show users whichever answer comes back first.
questions.explanation: Routing sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it well, which cuts cost while keeping quality on the hard 15% (B). Accept the routing errors you measure on an eval set, and escalate when the small model's answer fails a check. Using the cheapest model for everything hurts the hard cases (A). Users can't judge complexity reliably (C). Calling both models doubles the cost (D).

questions.stem: A chat assistant must check every user message for policy violations before answering. Running the check first and then answering adds 600 ms. How can you keep the check without the extra wait?
options: Skip the check for returning users, since they have already passed it in earlier conversations.
Run the check and the answer at the same time, and block the answer if the check fails.
Run the check only on every tenth message, which cuts the average delay by 90%.
Move the check to a nightly batch job that reviews all of the day's conversations together.
questions.explanation: Parallelization lets the guardrail and the answer run together. If the check fails, the answer is withheld, so safety is kept without adding the check's time on top (B). Returning users can still send harmful messages (A). Sampling lets 9 out of 10 messages through unchecked (C). A nightly review finds problems after users have already seen the answers (D).

questions.stem: A team is building a custom agent that reads files, runs shell commands, searches the web and manages long sessions. They are about to write their own loop, tool runner and context management on top of the raw Messages API. What should they consider first?
options: Writing the loop from scratch, since only fully custom code gives an agent complete control over its tools.
The Claude Agent SDK, which provides the agent loop, built-in tools, permissions and context management.
Driving the interactive Claude Code terminal from a script that types prompts and reads the screen, since it already has the tools.
A single very long prompt that tells the model to imagine the results of each tool call.
questions.explanation: The Agent SDK packages the same building blocks that power Claude Code: the tool loop, file and shell tools, permission controls and context management. That saves rebuilding them (B). Custom code is possible but repeats solved problems (A). Scripting the interactive terminal (C) is brittle; the SDK exposes the same capabilities programmatically. Imagined tool results aren't real results (D).

questions.stem: A developer is surprised that their chatbot 'forgets' what the user said two messages ago. Each request sends only the newest user message to the Messages API. What is the cause?
options: The model's context window is too small to hold more than one message at a time.
The API doesn't remember past requests, so the app must send the conversation history each time.
The conversation memory setting is turned off by default and must be switched on in the API console.
The model forgets earlier messages after about a minute unless prompt caching is turned on for the chat.
questions.explanation: The Messages API is stateless: each request stands alone. The application must store the conversation and send the relevant history with every request (B). Context windows hold far more than one message (A). There's no memory switch in the API (C). Prompt caching saves cost on repeated content but doesn't store conversations for you (D).

questions.stem: A document-processing workflow has six steps and takes 20 minutes per file. When step 5 fails because of a network error, the whole file starts again from step 1, repeating expensive model calls. What design fixes this?
options: Run all six steps in a single model call, so there is only one point where a failure can happen.
Save each step's output when it finishes, so a retry resumes from the step that failed.
Add a longer timeout to step 5, so network errors stop happening in that step.
Process files at night, when network errors happen less often.
questions.explanation: Checkpointing each step's result lets the workflow resume where it stopped instead of repeating finished work (B). One giant call makes failures more costly and harder to debug (A). A longer timeout doesn't prevent other failures (C). Running at night may reduce failures but doesn't fix the restart cost (D).

questions.stem: An autonomous research agent once ran for 6 hours and made 900 tool calls on a task that normally needs about 40, running up a large bill. What control should have been in place?
options: A system prompt line asking the agent to work efficiently, keep its research focused, and avoid unnecessary tool calls.
Hard limits in code on steps, tokens or cost per task, stopping the run and reporting when one is hit.
A larger model, since smarter models finish tasks faster and make fewer tool calls overall.
A weekly cost report sent to the team, so unusual spending is noticed and investigated.
questions.explanation: Agents can loop, so limits on steps, tokens, time or cost must be enforced in code, with a clear stop-and-report when one is reached (B). A prompt request isn't a limit (A). A bigger model may still loop (C). A weekly report finds the overrun long after it happened (D).

questions.stem: An HR agent has one tool called hr_action(action, data) that can look up policies, update addresses, change salaries or terminate employees, depending on the action text. Which redesign is best?
options: Keep the single tool, but list every allowed action in its description in much more detail.
Split it into separate tools with clear names and inputs, and put risky ones behind approval or remove them.
Keep the single tool, and ask the model to repeat the action back before running it.
Rename the tool to hr_safe_action, so the model treats every action it takes through the tool more carefully than it does today.
questions.explanation: Separate, focused tools are easier for the model to choose correctly, and they let you apply different permissions: lookups run freely, while salary changes or terminations need approval or aren't offered at all (B). A longer description still bundles dangerous and harmless actions together (A). Repeating the action back is a soft check (C). A name doesn't change what the tool can do (D).

questions.stem: A shipping tool returns 'Error 400' when the model passes a date in the wrong format. The agent keeps retrying with the same wrong date. What change helps the agent fix its own mistake?
options: Hide errors from the model and quietly retry the same request three more times.
Return a clear error message that says what was wrong and gives the expected format, such as YYYY-MM-DD.
Stop the agent whenever any tool returns an error, so that no bad or partial data can get into the shipping system.
Add the date format to the system prompt and leave the tool's error message as it is.
questions.explanation: Models act on what tools tell them. An error that explains the problem and the expected format lets the agent correct the input on the next try (B). Hidden retries repeat the same mistake (A). Stopping on every error ends tasks that could easily recover (C). A prompt note helps but the vague error still gives the model nothing to act on when it gets it wrong (D).

questions.stem: Users ask a research assistant for reports that take about 10 minutes to produce. The web app keeps the browser request open while it waits, and many requests time out. What design fits better?
options: Raise the web server's timeout to 15 minutes, so the browser requests stay open long enough for every report to finish.
Start a background job, return a job ID right away, and notify the user or let them check when it's done.
Ask users not to close or refresh the page until the report has fully finished.
Make the reports shorter so that every one of them finishes in under 30 seconds.
questions.explanation: Long tasks belong in an asynchronous job: accept the request, return an ID, do the work in the background, and notify or let users check progress (B). A 15-minute open request is fragile and ties up servers (A). Relying on users not to refresh fails often (C). Shorter reports change the product instead of fixing the design (D).

questions.stem: A software company sells a Claude-based assistant to 300 business customers. Each customer wants its own company name, tone and a few custom rules. Today each customer has a separate copy of the full prompt, and fixes must be made 300 times. What is a better design?
options: Keep separate copies, but assign one engineer to update all 300 copies by hand whenever a fix is made to any of them.
Use one shared base prompt plus a small per-customer settings block that fills in name, tone and rules.
Let each customer write and edit their entire prompt themselves, with no shared base prompt.
Fine-tune a separate model for each customer, so that no per-customer prompt is needed at all.
questions.explanation: A shared base prompt with per-customer variables keeps one place to fix and test, while still allowing customization. It also keeps a stable shared prefix that can be cached (B). 300 copies guarantee drift (A). Letting customers edit everything removes your safety and quality rules (C). Separate fine-tuned models are expensive and unnecessary for names, tone and a few rules (D).

questions.stem: A pipeline needs to pull the order number from 2 million emails a day. Order numbers always look like 'ORD-' followed by 8 digits. What is the best approach?
options: Send every email to Claude with a prompt asking it to find and return the order number.
Use a simple pattern match in code, and send only the emails where the pattern fails to Claude.
Fine-tune a small model to extract order numbers, so the cost per email ends up lower than using the API.
Ask customers to paste the order number into a separate form field on the website.
questions.explanation: When a fixed pattern describes the data, code is faster, cheaper and exact. Use the model only for the leftovers, such as typos or missing prefixes (B). Sending 2 million emails a day to a model is wasteful (A). Fine-tuning is unnecessary for a fixed pattern (C). A form change doesn't help with emails already arriving (D).

questions.stem: A coding assistant loads the whole repository, about 400,000 tokens, into every request 'so it has full context.' Responses are slow, expensive and often miss the relevant file. What approach is better?
options: Load the repository twice in each request, so the relevant files appear more often.
Give the model search and file-reading tools, so it loads only the files it needs for each task.
Remove all code comments from the files, so the whole repository fits in fewer tokens.
Load only the 20 largest files, since the most important code usually lives in the biggest files.
questions.explanation: Just-in-time context lets the model find and read what it needs through tools, instead of preloading everything. That keeps the context small and focused (B). Duplicating content adds cost and noise (A). Removing comments saves little and loses useful information (C). File size doesn't show which file matters for a task (D).

questions.stem: An orchestrator sends 'research the competitor's pricing' to three subagents. Each one returns overlapping results in different formats, and two of them researched the same pages. What change helps most?
options: Use one subagent instead of three, so that no work is ever duplicated.
Give each subagent a distinct scope, a required output format, and what to leave out.
Ask the subagents to message each other while they work, so they can split the task themselves.
Let the orchestrator remove duplicate results at the end, and keep the instructions the same.
questions.explanation: Subagents only know what the orchestrator tells them. Clear boundaries (which competitor, region or source), a fixed output format and explicit exclusions prevent overlap and make the results easy to combine (B). One subagent loses the parallelism (A). Subagents report to the orchestrator and don't coordinate with each other (C). Removing duplicates at the end still pays for the duplicated work (D).

questions.stem: A travel assistant must answer 'Is my flight on time right now?' The model's training data ends months before today. What is required?
options: A newer model with a more recent training cutoff, which brings what it knows closer to the present day.
A tool that looks up live flight status, with the model answering from the tool's result.
A system prompt line telling the model to make its best guess about current delays from typical flight patterns.
Fine-tuning the model on last month's flight data, so it knows recent patterns.
questions.explanation: Live, changing facts can't come from training data, which is fixed at a cutoff date. The model needs a tool that fetches current data and answers from it (B). Even the newest model's training data ends months before today, so it can't know today's flights (A). A guess is a made-up answer (C). Last month's data is still out of date (D).

questions.stem: An insurer wants Claude to read photos of damaged cars and scanned repair estimates. Some photos are blurry and some estimates are handwritten. What should the design plan include?
options: Nothing special, since Claude reads all images perfectly regardless of their quality.
A test set of real photos and scans, including poor ones, and a human check when the image is unclear.
Converting every image to black and white before sending it, so the model can read the details more accurately.
Using text-only processing, since images can't be sent to Claude through the API.
questions.explanation: Claude can read images, but accuracy drops on blurry photos and messy handwriting. Test on realistic samples, including bad ones, and route unclear cases to a person (B). Image quality matters (A). Black-and-white conversion can remove useful detail (C). The API does accept images (D).

questions.stem: An analyst team wants an agent that researches market trends using web search and writes a briefing. Which TWO design choices most improve how much the team can trust the briefing?
options: Require a citation link for every factual claim, so analysts can check the source.
Require several independent sources for key claims, and flag claims backed by only one source.
Tell the agent to write with confidence, so the briefing doesn't seem uncertain to readers.
Limit the agent to the first search result for each query, to keep the research fast.
Ask the agent to fill any gaps in the sources from its own training knowledge.
questions.explanation: Citations let readers verify each claim (A), and cross-checking key claims across sources catches errors or biased sources, while flagging single-source claims shows where to be careful (B). Forced confidence hides uncertainty (C). One result per query is too thin (D). Filling gaps from training data mixes unverified and possibly outdated facts into the briefing (E).

questions.stem: A customer-service agent must remember a user's preferences, such as preferred language and delivery address, across conversations that happen weeks apart. What is the best design?
options: Send the full transcript of every past conversation with each new request.
Store a short set of preferences per user, and add them to the context at the start of each session.
Ask the user to repeat their language, address and other preferences at the start of each conversation, so they're current.
Rely on the model to remember users between conversations on its own.
questions.explanation: A small, structured memory store, retrieved at the start of each session, keeps what matters without flooding the context (B). Full transcripts grow without limit and cost more each time (A). Making users repeat themselves is poor service (C). The model doesn't remember anything between requests (D).

questions.stem: A team is choosing a model for a high-volume task: pulling 6 fields from typed invoices. A small, fast model scores 98.5% on their eval set, and the largest model scores 99.0% at 10 times the cost. What should they do?
options: Use the largest model, since the highest accuracy is the safest choice for anything financial, and the cost is acceptable.
Use the small model, and send invoices that fail a validation check to the larger model or a person.
Use the largest model for the first month, then switch to the small model once the team is sure it can save money.
Use neither, and build a custom extraction model from scratch for this task.
questions.explanation: A 0.5-point gain at 10 times the cost rarely pays off at high volume. Using the small model with a validation check, and escalating only the failures, gets close to the higher accuracy at a fraction of the cost (B). Bigger isn't automatically right (A). A month on the large model doesn't answer the question (C). Building a custom model is unnecessary (D).

questions.stem: A company wants Claude to draft replies to customer complaints. Replies will be sent automatically if the model is 'confident.' What is the main design flaw?
options: The model's own sense of confidence isn't a reliable signal for whether a reply is safe to send.
Complaint replies are usually too short and simple to benefit from using a language model in the first place.
Automatic sending is slower than having a person send the reply, so it removes the main benefit of automation.
Claude can't write in a polite tone without a large number of examples.
questions.explanation: A model saying it's confident doesn't mean it's right. Decide what can be sent automatically using checks in code and measured eval results by category, such as auto-sending only low-risk complaint types that meet a tested quality bar (A). The other options aren't real limitations (B, C, D).

questions.stem: A team is scoping an assistant that must answer questions about 500 product manuals and also check live inventory. Which TWO capabilities does the design need?
options: Retrieval over the product manuals, so answers come from the right manual sections.
A tool that queries the inventory system, so stock levels are current.
Fine-tuning on the manuals, so the model memorizes every specification.
A larger context window, so all 500 manuals fit into every request.
A prompt telling the model to estimate stock levels from past sales.
questions.explanation: The manuals are a large, mostly fixed body of text, so retrieval fits (A). Inventory changes constantly, so it needs a live lookup tool (B). Fine-tuning isn't a reliable way to store exact specifications (C). 500 manuals won't fit in one request efficiently (D). Estimated stock levels would be made-up answers (E).

questions.stem: A legal-tech startup wants an agent that takes a due-diligence request, works through a virtual data room of several thousand documents for two to six hours, writes interim findings, and lets a lawyer send follow-up instructions while it runs. The startup has four engineers, no platform team, and no experience running sandboxed compute. It needs the agent to run shell commands and Python against the documents. Which runtime choice fits best, and what must be confirmed before committing?
options: Claude Managed Agents, which provides the harness, sandboxes and stateful sessions; first confirm its data-retention terms fit client contracts.
The Messages API with a custom agent loop on the startup's own Kubernetes cluster, which gives the most control over sandboxing and lets the four engineers tune every part of the harness.
A single Messages API call with a 1M-token context and every document attached, since a long context removes the need for tools, sandboxes or a session to hold intermediate state.
Claude Code in headless mode on a developer laptop, triggered by cron, since it already runs shell commands and can be left running for hours against the data room.
questions.explanation: Long-running, asynchronous work that needs a sandbox and mid-run steering is the case Managed Agents is built for, and a four-person team without platform experience gains the most from a hosted harness (A). Because sessions persist transcripts and sandbox state server-side, retention and eligibility for programs like zero data retention must be checked against client terms first. Building a custom loop and sandbox on Kubernetes (B) is the fine-grained-control option, but it is the infrastructure the team can't staff. Thousands of documents don't fit one request, and analysis needs code execution (C). A laptop on cron (D) is not a production runtime for client data.

questions.stem: A platform team is choosing where each of three workloads should run. Match each workload to the best deployment surface or runtime.
choices: The Messages API with an application-owned agent loop
Claude Managed Agents
Claude Code with project settings and hooks
The Message Batches API
rows: A customer-support chat that must answer within 2 seconds, call four internal tools, and log every step in the company's existing tracing system.
A nightly job that drafts summaries of 40,000 closed tickets, with results needed by the next morning.
An agent that refactors a client's repository over several hours in a sandbox, while a product manager checks progress and redirects it from a web app.
questions.explanation: Item 1: a latency-bound chat with custom tools and existing tracing needs the fine-grained control of an application-owned loop on the Messages API (A). Item 2: work that can wait until morning fits the Batches API, which costs about half as much (D). Item 3: hours-long sandboxed work with mid-run steering from a web app fits Managed Agents' stateful sessions (B). Claude Code with project settings (C) is aimed at developers working in their own repositories, not at a product manager steering an agent from a web app.

questions.stem: An insurer wants Claude to help with subrogation: deciding whether another party's insurer should repay a claim. Today an adjuster reads the file, identifies the at-fault party, calculates the recoverable amount from the policy and payment ledger, drafts a demand letter, and sends it after a supervisor's approval for amounts above $25,000. Errors in the amount create regulatory complaints. The sponsor asks which parts should go to Claude. What is the strongest division of work?
options: Claude identifies the at-fault party and calculates the recoverable amount, since both steps need judgment; the adjuster drafts and sends each letter after a supervisor approves larger amounts.
Claude does every step end to end, including sending letters, and a supervisor spot-checks a 10% sample each week, which keeps review costs predictable as volume grows.
Claude proposes the at-fault party with cited evidence; code computes the amount from the ledger; Claude drafts the letter; the adjuster confirms and the supervisor approves above $25,000.
Keep the whole process manual, because regulatory complaints mean no part of the workflow can be delegated to an AI system safely.
questions.explanation: Delegate by reliability: Claude is strong at reading files and drafting, and its findings can be checked through cited evidence; exact money arithmetic belongs in code; accountability and the regulatory approval stay with people (C). Having Claude calculate the amount (A) puts the step most likely to trigger complaints on probabilistic arithmetic. End-to-end automation with sampling (B) removes the required approval above $25,000. Refusing all delegation (D) ignores the low-risk reading and drafting work that can be checked.

questions.stem: A retailer runs a returns agent built on the Messages API. It calls tools to look up orders, check return eligibility and issue refunds up to $200. Larger refunds go to a human queue. The architect is reviewing which responsibilities belong to the model and which belong to the surrounding system. For each statement, select Yes if it is a sound design choice.
statements: The $200 refund limit is enforced in the refund tool's code, not only described in the system prompt.
The model decides on its own whether a refund request is large enough to need the human queue, using its judgment of the customer's tone.
Eligibility rules that change every quarter are read from the policy system by the eligibility tool, so prompts don't need editing when rules change.
questions.explanation: Statement 1: Yes. Limits on money movement must be enforced in code, because a prompt instruction can be ignored or manipulated. Statement 2: No. Routing to the human queue should follow a deterministic rule on the amount, not the model's reading of tone. Statement 3: Yes. Keeping fast-changing rules in the system of record, behind a tool, avoids prompt edits and keeps one source of truth.

questions.stem: A bank's architecture review asks you to justify a design in which three Claude calls run in sequence: classify an incoming complaint, retrieve the relevant policy, then draft a reply for an agent to review. A reviewer argues that one agent with all three tools would be 'more modern and flexible.' Complaint volume is 9,000 a day, the steps never change order, and the regulator expects an audit trail showing which policy each reply relied on. What is the best response?
options: Switch to the single agent, since letting the model decide the order of the steps makes the system more flexible as new complaint types appear.
Switch to an orchestrator with three worker agents, so the classification, retrieval and drafting steps can run in parallel and finish sooner.
Keep the workflow but let the model skip the retrieval step when it is confident it already knows the policy, which reduces latency on the most common complaint types.
Keep the fixed workflow: the order never changes, it is cheaper and easier to test at this volume, and each step's output is the audit trail.
questions.explanation: When the steps and their order are known in advance, a workflow is cheaper, more predictable and easier to audit than an agent, and here the audit trail is a regulatory requirement (D). Model-chosen ordering (A) adds cost and variance for flexibility the process doesn't need. The steps depend on each other, so they can't run in parallel (B). Skipping retrieval (C) breaks the audit requirement that every reply shows its policy source.

questions.stem: A client's operations agent runs on Claude Managed Agents. It connects to the client's ticketing system through an MCP server and runs remediation scripts in its sandbox. The security team asks where the credentials for the ticketing system should live, and how the agent should reach an internal MCP server that is not exposed to the internet. Which approach fits the platform?
options: Paste the ticketing credentials into the agent's system prompt, so the agent can pass them to the MCP server whenever it needs to authenticate.
Store the credentials in the platform's vault for MCP authentication, and reach the private server through an MCP tunnel.
Expose the internal MCP server on a public URL protected by an IP allowlist, and store the credentials in a file inside the agent's sandbox environment.
Run a copy of the ticketing database inside each session's sandbox, so the agent never needs credentials or network access to the real system.
questions.explanation: Managed Agents keeps MCP credentials out of the model's context in a vault, and it can reach private MCP servers through MCP tunnels, so the internal server stays off the public internet (B). Credentials in the system prompt (A) can leak through outputs and logs. A public URL and a credentials file in the sandbox (C) widen the attack surface for no reason. A database copy per session (D) creates stale, ungoverned copies of production data and can't update the real tickets.

questions.stem: A hospital group wants Claude to help nurses write shift-handoff notes from the electronic health record. The CNO's stated goal is 'save nurses time.' In discovery you learn that handoff errors are the hospital's top patient-safety concern, nurses spend about 25 minutes per handoff, and the EHR vendor allows read access through an approved API only. Which requirement statement should anchor the design?
options: Draft handoff notes from EHR data via the approved API, cut handoff time to about 10 minutes, and keep or improve the critical-item omission rate versus nurse-written notes.
Generate a complete handoff note for every patient in under 30 seconds using the newest available model, so nurses can sign off each note without needing to read it through first.
Replace the handoff conversation with an AI-written summary, since a written note is more consistent than a verbal handoff and removes human error from the process.
Let nurses ask free-form questions about any patient during the shift, so the assistant covers handoffs and also every other information need that comes up in the hospital.
questions.explanation: A good requirement turns the stated goal into measurable outcomes and includes the constraint that matters most, which here is patient safety, plus the integration limit (A). Sign-off without reading (B) removes the safety check the hospital most needs. Replacing the conversation (C) overreaches the brief and treats the model as error-free. A general assistant (D) expands scope far beyond the handoff problem and its measurable value.

questions.stem: An agent drafts quarterly board reports by pulling figures from five finance systems. After launch, the finance team finds that when one source system is down, the agent still produces a confident report and fills the missing section with plausible numbers from earlier quarters it saw in its context. The CFO wants a design change, not just a prompt tweak. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Add a system-prompt rule that the agent must not reuse figures from earlier quarters, and repeat the rule at the end of every tool result it receives.
Lower the temperature to 0 so the agent stops inventing numbers when data is missing, and add a disclaimer about data freshness to the report's cover page for the board.
Switch to a larger model, since a more capable model can tell the difference between current figures and figures from earlier quarters that it saw in its context.
Make each tool return an explicit error when its system is unavailable, and have code block report assembly until every section has fresh, sourced data.
questions.explanation: The root cause is that a missing source isn't surfaced as a failure, so the agent fills the gap. Explicit error results plus a code-enforced completeness gate stop a report from being assembled on missing data (D). A prompt rule (A) is the tweak the CFO ruled out and can still be ignored. Temperature (B) doesn't stop the model from filling gaps, and a disclaimer doesn't fix the numbers. A larger model (C) still has no fresh data to report.

questions.stem: An architect is reviewing three proposed Claude features for a logistics company. Match each feature to the architecture pattern that fits it best.
choices: A fixed, code-defined workflow of model calls
An autonomous agent with tools
A single model call with structured output
Retrieval-augmented generation over a document index
rows: Extract shipper, consignee, weight and incoterms from each scanned bill of lading into the ERP's schema.
Answer drivers' questions from 4,000 pages of safety and route procedures that change monthly.
Investigate a delayed shipment by checking tracking, warehouse logs and carrier messages, where the next step depends on what each source shows.
questions.explanation: Row 1: pulling fixed fields from one document into a schema is a single call with structured output (C). Row 2: answering from a large, changing document set calls for retrieval over an index (D). Row 3: an investigation whose next step depends on what it finds is the case where an agent earns its cost (B). A fixed workflow (A) fits multi-step processes whose steps are known in advance, which none of these is.

questions.stem: A university wants a Claude-based assistant that answers students' questions about financial aid. Aid rules are in 300 policy pages, each student's award is in the student information system, and decisions about appeals are made by aid officers. For each design decision, select Yes if it is sound.
statements: The assistant retrieves policy text to answer general questions and calls a tool for the signed-in student's own award details.
The assistant decides financial-aid appeals itself when the student's explanation is persuasive, to reduce the officers' backlog.
Questions the assistant can't answer from policy or the student's record are routed to an aid officer with the conversation attached.
questions.explanation: Statement 1: Yes. General rules come from retrieval, and personal data comes from a tool scoped to the authenticated student. Statement 2: No. Appeal decisions belong to aid officers; the assistant can summarize an appeal but shouldn't decide it. Statement 3: Yes. A clear escalation path with context is part of a sound design.

questions.stem: A team is writing non-functional requirements for a contract-review assistant. Match each stakeholder concern to the requirement that best captures it.
choices: p95 time to first token under 2 seconds, measured at the client
Every finding cites the clause it is based on
Monthly model and infrastructure cost under an agreed budget per contract
Contract text is processed only in the client's approved cloud region
rows: The general counsel says lawyers won't trust a finding they can't check quickly against the contract.
The CFO wants to know the assistant will stay affordable as contract volume triples next year.
The data protection officer says client contracts can't leave the EU.
questions.explanation: Row 1: trust through quick checking becomes a citation requirement (B). Row 2: affordability at growing volume becomes a cost-per-contract budget (C). Row 3: the EU restriction becomes a processing-region requirement (D). The latency requirement (A) is a valid non-functional requirement, but none of these three stakeholders raised speed.

questions.stem: A support platform handles about 1M requests a day. About 80% are simple intents (order status, password reset, shipping policy) and 20% need multi-step reasoning across account history. Leadership wants lower cost without hurting resolution quality on the hard cases. Which model strategy is most defensible?
options: Use the most capable model for all traffic and offset cost with prompt caching, since a single model is simpler to evaluate and keeps quality uniform.
Use the smallest model for all traffic and add detailed reasoning instructions and examples for the complex intents, keeping the architecture simple.
Offer users a 'quick answer' versus 'detailed answer' choice in the UI that selects the model, letting demand reveal the right split.
