options: About 3 days, because 800 requests a day easily covers the 2,500 drafts needed
About 31 days, because only about 80 eligible drafts arrive each day
About 7 days, because one full week covers the weekday and weekend patterns that a test needs.
About 300 days, because each draft must be reviewed by a person
questions.explanation: Only eligible requests count toward the sample: 10% of 800 is 80 RFP drafts a day, and 2,500 ÷ 80 ≈ 31 days (B). Counting all 800 requests overstates the sample (A). A week is a minimum for covering weekday patterns, not a substitute for the required sample (C). Grading method doesn't change the arithmetic (D).

questions.stem: An A/B test compares two retrieval setups. The document collection mixes 5-page memos and 80-page reports across six practice areas, and users have different document permissions. Which TWO steps best keep the two groups comparable?
options: Randomize assignment within each practice area and permission profile, so both versions get the same mix.
Run both versions during the same weeks, instead of the old setup one month and the new setup the next.
Send questions about long 80-page reports to the new setup, since it was built to handle them better.
Let consultants opt in to the new setup, so the most interested users give the most useful feedback.
Leave out users with restricted permissions, since their limited access makes the results noisier.
questions.explanation: Stratified randomization guarantees the same mix of practice areas and permission levels in both groups (A). Running both versions at the same time stops changes over time, such as new questions or new documents, from being mistaken for a treatment effect (B). Routing hard questions to one version (C) or letting users choose (D) creates biased groups. Dropping restricted users means the test no longer represents real usage (E).

questions.stem: Three days into a test planned for four weeks, the new prompt leads 78% to 70%, and the dashboard shows p < 0.05. The sponsor wants to stop the test and ship. What is the best response?
options: Ship now, because a p-value under 0.05 means there is less than a 5% chance the result is wrong.
Keep running to the planned sample, because stopping at the first good result inflates false positives.
Stop the test and restart it with a new success metric that better fits what the early data is showing.
Ship to half the users now and keep the other half on the old prompt permanently, as an ongoing control group.
questions.explanation: Checking repeatedly and stopping at the first significant result raises the real false-positive rate well above 5%, and early leads often shrink as more data arrives (B). (A) misreads the p-value and ignores the effect of peeking. Changing the metric after seeing data invites false conclusions (C). An indefinite split delays the decision and doesn't answer the question (D).

questions.stem: A team tests moving a simple formatting task from Sonnet to Haiku. Cost per request is expected to fall about 70%, and output quality is expected to stay the same. How should they classify the expected effect when planning the test?
options: Small effect, because the quality of the formatted output is expected to stay about the same.
Large effect on cost, the primary metric, with quality as a guardrail that must not drop.
No measurable effect, because cost is an accounting figure rather than a change in model behavior.
Unknown effect, because Sonnet and Haiku can't be compared fairly on the same task.
questions.explanation: Effect size is judged on the primary metric, meaning what the change is meant to move. Here that's cost, and a 70% drop is a large effect (B). Quality is the guardrail you check for no drop, not the effect being tested, so (A) uses the wrong metric. Cost is directly measurable from usage logs (C), and the two models can be compared on the same eval set (D).

questions.stem: Two changes have the same small expected effect. Change 1 rewords a greeting in a low-stakes FAQ bot. Change 2 restructures the prompt of a medical intake summarizer, where a missed allergy could delay treatment. Why does change 2 need far more evidence before shipping?
options: Restructuring a prompt produces a larger effect than rewording a single message, so it needs a bigger sample to detect.
A wrong call there could harm patients and can't be undone, which raises the confidence required.
Medical text is longer, so each sample carries less information and more samples are needed.
Regulators require exactly 99% confidence for every healthcare change, whatever the stakes or the effect size.
questions.explanation: The confidence requirement is set by the consequence of a wrong call and how reversible it is, independent of effect size. Delayed treatment is serious and can't be undone, so it needs high confidence and a larger sample (B). The effect sizes are the same by premise (A). Text length doesn't set the confidence requirement (C). There is no fixed 99% regulatory rule (D).

questions.stem: A cost model multiplies 24,000 monthly requests by an average of 5,200 input tokens and lands at 40% of the budget. Retrieved context per request actually ranges from about 1,000 tokens (short memos) to 40,000 tokens (long reports). What should you do before declaring the system within budget?
options: Nothing: with 24,000 requests, the average is reliable and the expensive requests cancel out.
Model cost from the real spread of context sizes, including the expensive tail, and test a worst-case mix.
Double the estimate as a safety margin, since cost estimates are usually off by about half.
Move the whole workload to the cheapest model so that the expensive requests no longer matter.
questions.explanation: A flat average assumes requests cluster near the mean. With context sizes from 1,000 to 40,000 tokens, a tail of large requests can push real cost far above the estimate, so model the actual distribution and test a worst-case mix (B). Large requests don't cancel out (A). An arbitrary multiplier isn't analysis (C). Switching models changes quality and doesn't answer whether this design fits the budget (D).

questions.stem: A support assistant's eval set was built 9 months ago from launch-day questions. It still scores 95%, but customer complaints have risen since a new product line launched. What is the most likely problem with the eval?
options: The eval set is too large, so problems are hidden among too many easy questions.
The eval set no longer reflects what users ask now, so add recent real questions, including the new product line.
The scoring method is broken and should be replaced with a newer LLM judge right away, since the score hasn't moved in nine months.
95% is too high a score to be trusted, so the threshold should be raised to 99%.
questions.explanation: An eval set built from old traffic stops representing current use. Regularly add recent production questions, especially new topics, so the eval tracks what users actually ask (B). Size isn't the issue (A). Nothing points to a broken scorer (C). Raising the threshold doesn't add the missing questions (D).

questions.stem: An engineer tweaks a prompt 40 times, re-running the same 150-question eval set after each change, until the score reaches 97%. In production, accuracy is about 88%. What went wrong?
options: The production model is a different, lower-quality version from the one used in testing, which explains the nine-point gap.
The prompt was tuned to fit the 150 questions; a separate held-out test set was needed to check real performance.
150 questions is too many, which made the eval results unstable from run to run.
The engineer should have tweaked the prompt more times, until it reached 100%.
questions.explanation: Repeatedly tuning against the same questions fits the prompt to those questions. Keep a held-out set that's never used for tuning, and use it to estimate real performance (B). Nothing suggests a different model (A). 150 is a reasonable size (C). More tuning on the same set makes the overfitting worse (D).

questions.stem: Two expert reviewers label the same 200 contract clauses as 'risky' or 'not risky' and disagree on 22% of them. The team's target for the model is 98% agreement with the reviewers. What should happen?
options: Keep the 98% target, since the model should be held to a higher standard than people.
Clarify the labeling rules until reviewers agree more, then set a target the reference labels can support.
Use only the first reviewer's labels and ignore the second reviewer's, since the two of them disagree so often.
Replace both reviewers with an LLM judge, which gives the same label on every run and removes the disagreement.
questions.explanation: If experts disagree 22% of the time, the labels themselves are uncertain, and 98% agreement isn't meaningful. Tighten the rubric with examples until reviewers agree more, then set realistic targets (B). The target can't exceed what the reference can support (A). Picking one reviewer hides the problem (C). A judge that agrees with itself doesn't make the labels right (D).

questions.stem: An LLM judge scores customer replies from 1 to 5. Reviewers notice it gives higher scores to longer replies, even when shorter ones are better. What helps most?
options: Use a longer judge prompt, so the judge has more instructions to follow.
Give the judge a specific rubric that rewards required content, says length isn't a goal, and check it against human scores.
Truncate all replies to the same length before the judge sees them.
Average the judge's scores with a random number to cancel out the length bias.
questions.explanation: Judges have biases, such as favoring longer answers. A rubric that defines what earns points and states length isn't a goal, checked against human-scored examples, reduces the bias and shows how well it works (B). A longer prompt doesn't fix the criteria (A). Truncation cuts off real content (C). Adding randomness adds noise (D).

questions.stem: An eval checks whether an extraction prompt outputs valid JSON with a correct invoice date. The team currently uses an LLM judge for both checks. What is a better approach?
options: Keep using the LLM judge, since judges are more flexible than code for every kind of check, including dates.
Check JSON validity and the exact date with code, and save LLM judges for things code can't check.
Have a person review every output by hand, since code can't check dates correctly.
Drop the date check and only check that the JSON is valid, since date errors are rare in typed invoices.
questions.explanation: When a check has a clear right answer, such as valid JSON or an exact date, code is cheaper, faster and fully consistent. LLM judges are for qualities like tone or completeness (B). Using a judge here adds cost and variation (A). Code compares dates easily (C). Dropping the date check misses errors (D).

questions.stem: An agent handles refund requests over several turns, using tools to update the order system. How should the eval decide whether a test conversation succeeded?
options: Check whether the agent's last message says the refund was processed.
Check the final state of the test order system: the right refund, amount and status, and no unwanted changes.
Count how many turns each test conversation took, since shorter conversations mean the agent resolved the refund successfully.
Ask the agent at the end whether it thinks the task went well, and record its answer.
questions.explanation: For agents that change things, the reliable test is the outcome: inspect the system state after the conversation, including that nothing else was changed (B). The agent can claim success without actually achieving it (A, D). Turn count measures efficiency, not success (C).

questions.stem: An agent solved a test task correctly, but it took a very different path from the 'expected' sequence of tool calls in the test. The eval marked it as failed. What should change?
options: Nothing: agents should follow the exact expected sequence of tool calls, so marking this run as a failure is correct.
Grade mainly on whether the outcome is correct, and separately track cost or steps instead of requiring one path.
Remove all agent tests from the eval, since agents can't be tested reliably.
Add more expected paths to the test until this run is counted as a pass.
questions.explanation: Agents can solve a task in many valid ways. Grading the outcome avoids penalizing good alternatives, while tracking steps or cost catches wasteful ones (B). Requiring one path makes tests fragile (A). Agents can be tested, with outcome checks (C). Listing every path doesn't scale (D).

questions.stem: An agent completes a task correctly in 1 of 4 tries on some tests. For a customer-facing workflow, the agent must succeed every time it's run. Which metric reflects that need?
options: pass@4, the chance that at least one of four tries succeeds.
pass^4, the chance that all four tries succeed.
Average tokens per try, since cheaper tries are more reliable.
The best score out of the four tries.
questions.explanation: pass@k rewards succeeding at least once in k tries, which fits when a person can pick the best result. pass^k requires every try to succeed, which matches 'must work every time' (B). pass@4 would overstate reliability here (A). Token use isn't reliability (C). The best of four hides the failures (D).

questions.stem: A team sends every question to a small model first and escalates to a large model when the small model's answer fails a validation check. How should they judge whether this setup is better than using the large model for everything?
options: By checking that the small model answers more than half of the questions on its own.
By comparing overall accuracy and total cost on the same eval set for both setups.
By measuring the small model's accuracy alone, since the large model is already known to be good.
By counting how many questions escalate, since fewer escalations means the small model is handling more of the load.
questions.explanation: A cascade only makes sense if it gives similar accuracy at lower cost, or better value overall, so compare both setups end to end on the same eval set (B). Share handled (A), the small model alone (C) or the escalation count (D) each miss part of the picture.

questions.stem: Several engineers edit prompts for a production assistant, and twice a change has quietly broken an important use case. What process change catches this before release?
options: Ask engineers to test their changes by hand on a few example questions they choose themselves, before each prompt change goes out.
Run the eval suite automatically on every prompt change, and block the release if key scores drop.
Allow prompt changes only on Fridays, so problems can be fixed over the weekend.
Keep a changelog of prompt edits so the team knows who to ask after a break.
questions.explanation: Automated eval checks on every change, with release gates on key metrics, catch regressions before users see them (B). Hand-picked tests miss the cases people don't think of (A). The day of the week doesn't catch anything (C). A changelog helps after the fact but doesn't prevent the break (D).

questions.stem: An assistant passed all offline evals at launch. How should the team keep track of quality in production?
options: Re-run the same launch eval set once a year, and compare each year's score with the score the assistant got at launch.
Regularly sample real conversations, score them with checks or a judge, and have people review a share.
Track the number of thumbs-down clicks, since unhappy users are the ones most likely to report a problem.
Assume quality stays the same, since the model and prompt haven't changed.
questions.explanation: Production questions change over time. Ongoing sampling and scoring of real traffic, with human review of a share of it, catches drift and new failure types (B). A yearly re-run of old questions misses new topics (A). Most unhappy users never click thumbs-down (C). Inputs and data change even when the model doesn't (D).

questions.stem: After a safety update, a medical-information assistant now correctly refuses more harmful requests, but it also refuses many harmless ones, such as 'What is a normal resting heart rate?' What should the eval add?
options: Nothing: refusing more often is the safer choice for a medical assistant, even when some harmless questions get refused too.
A set of harmless questions that sound sensitive, to measure how often the assistant refuses them wrongly.
A measure of how polite the refusals are, so they sound kinder to users.
Fewer harmful test prompts, so the refusal rate on them looks lower.
questions.explanation: Safety evals should measure both sides: harmful requests that should be refused, and harmless but sensitive-sounding ones that should be answered. Over-refusal fails users too (B). Refusing everything isn't safe or useful (A). Politeness doesn't fix wrong refusals (C). Removing tests hides the problem (D).

questions.stem: A team tests a new prompt on 100 questions and gets 82% correct. A manager asks how confident they can be that the true accuracy is about 82%. What is a fair answer?
options: It's exactly 82%, since every one of the 100 questions was graded carefully and the grading itself didn't contain any errors.
Roughly plus or minus 8 points, so the true accuracy could be anywhere from the mid-70s to about 90%.
Plus or minus 1 point, since 100 questions is a large sample for an eval.
It can't be estimated at all without testing every possible user question.
questions.explanation: With 100 items, the 95% margin of error is about ±1.96 × √(0.82 × 0.18 / 100), roughly ±7.5 points. Small eval sets give wide ranges, so small differences between prompts may not be real (B). It isn't exact (A) or that tight (C), and a reasonable estimate doesn't need every possible question (D).

questions.stem: A new prompt raises overall accuracy from 88% to 90%. Broken down by language, English improved, but Spanish dropped from 87% to 79%. Spanish speakers are 20% of users. What should happen before shipping?
options: Ship, since the overall score went up and English speakers are the majority of users.
Investigate and fix the Spanish drop, since an overall gain can hide a serious drop for a group.
Remove the Spanish questions from the eval set, since they're the part that is pulling the overall score down.
Ship to English speakers only and stop supporting Spanish until the next release.
questions.explanation: An overall score can hide a large drop in one group. An 8-point drop for 20% of users is a real regression, so fix it or ship to segments separately (B). Shipping ignores it (A). Removing the questions hides it (C). Dropping a language you support is a business decision, not a fix (D).

questions.stem: A citation-heavy research assistant passes an eval that checks whether each answer includes citations. Users still find that some citations don't actually support the claim next to them. What should the eval check?
options: That every answer includes at least three separate citations.
That each cited passage actually supports the specific claim it's attached to.
That every citation links to a page that loads without an error.
That the citations are formatted in one consistent style throughout every answer the assistant gives.
questions.explanation: Having citations isn't the same as having correct ones. Check that each cited source supports its claim, using a judge, code that compares the text, or human review (B). More citations (A), working links (C) or tidy formatting (D) don't show the source backs the claim.

questions.stem: A team needs 500 test questions for a new insurance assistant but has only 40 real examples. They plan to have Claude write 460 more. What makes this approach sound?
options: Use the 460 generated questions as they are, since the model writes realistic questions that cover the same ground as real customers.
Have Claude draft them from the real examples and edge-case lists, and have domain experts review and fix them.
Generate 5,000 questions instead, since a larger eval set gives a more stable score than a small reviewed one.
Generate the questions and their expected answers with the same model being tested, then spot-check a few.
questions.explanation: Generated questions are a fast start, but they need expert review for realism, correct answers and coverage of hard cases (B). Unreviewed questions can be unrealistic or wrong (A). Quantity doesn't fix quality (C). Answers written by the model under test can share its mistakes and inflate scores (D).

questions.stem: A full eval suite of 3,000 cases costs about $90 and takes 40 minutes. Engineers want feedback on every commit, which happens dozens of times a day. What is a sensible setup?
options: Run all 3,000 cases on every commit, and accept the cost and the waiting time.
Run a small, fast set of key cases on every commit, and the full suite nightly and before each release.
Run the eval suite only once a month, to keep costs as low as possible.
Skip evals for small prompt edits, since small wording changes to a prompt rarely cause regressions in quality.
questions.explanation: Tiered evals balance speed and coverage: a quick set of critical cases on each commit catches obvious breaks, and the full suite catches the rest before release (B). Running everything on every commit is slow and costly (A). Monthly runs catch problems too late (C). Small edits can cause big regressions (D).

questions.stem: A team re-runs a 3,000-case eval every night with interactive API calls. Results aren't needed until the next morning. How can they cut the eval cost the most without changing the results?
options: Run only every other case, which halves the cost of each nightly run.
Submit the nightly run through the Message Batches API, which costs about half as much.
Switch the nightly eval to a smaller, cheaper model, so that each of the 3,000 test cases costs less to run.
Run the nightly eval at temperature 0, which shortens responses and so reduces the output tokens billed per case.
questions.explanation: Nightly evals don't need instant answers, so the Batches API's 50% discount fits perfectly, with the same model and the same cases (B). Running half the cases weakens the eval (A). A smaller model changes what you're measuring (C). Temperature changes randomness, not response length, so it doesn't cut the bill (D).

questions.stem: A team tests extended thinking budgets of 1,000, 4,000, 16,000 and 32,000 tokens on a reasoning task. Accuracy is 81%, 89%, 91% and 91.5%, and cost and latency rise with each step. Which budget should they pick?
options: 32,000, since it gives the highest accuracy of the four budgets tested, and accuracy matters more than cost on reasoning tasks.
Around 4,000 to 16,000, where the accuracy gains level off compared with the extra cost and delay.
1,000, since it is the cheapest and the fastest of the four options.
No thinking at all, since the gains don't justify any extra cost.
questions.explanation: Look for where the gains flatten: going from 1K to 4K adds 8 points, while 16K to 32K adds only half a point for much more cost and delay. Choose in the middle range, depending on how much each point is worth (B). Maximizing accuracy alone ignores cost (A). The cheapest option leaves a big gain on the table (C). The data shows thinking does help (D).

questions.stem: A summarizer's output costs dominate spending. Users read only the first paragraph, but summaries average 600 tokens. What change should the team test first?
options: Turn on prompt caching for the input documents, which cuts the input cost.
Ask for a 2 to 3 sentence summary and check on the eval set that quality holds.
Switch to the Batches API, since users can wait until the next day to read their finished summaries.
Raise max_tokens so that summaries aren't cut off in the middle, which forces users to request them again.
questions.explanation: Output is the main cost, and most of it isn't read. Asking for shorter summaries, and confirming on the eval set that they keep the key points, attacks the biggest cost directly (B). Caching only lowers input cost (A). Batches don't suit users waiting for summaries (C). A higher max_tokens doesn't lower cost (D).

questions.stem: A team uses Claude as a judge to compare two summary prompts. The judge sees both summaries side by side and picks the better one. Prompt B wins 64% of comparisons. A reviewer notices that B's summaries were always shown first, and that B's summaries are about 40% longer. Before trusting the result, what should the team change?
options: Nothing: 64% is well above 50% across many comparisons, so the result is significant whatever order the summaries were shown in.
Replace the judge with a larger model, since a more capable judge is less affected by the order and length of the summaries it compares.
Swap the order of each pair and score both orders, keep length out of the rubric, and check the judge against human ratings.
Ask the judge to explain its choice before picking, which removes position and length bias from its decisions.
questions.explanation: LLM judges can show position bias and a preference for longer answers. Scoring both orders, writing the rubric so length isn't rewarded, and calibrating against human ratings removes those confounds (C). A significant-looking result (A) can be produced entirely by the bias. A bigger judge (B) may reduce bias but doesn't show it's gone. Asking for reasoning first (D) can help consistency but doesn't remove order or length effects.

questions.stem: Anthropic has announced the retirement of the model behind a client's claims-triage system in four months. The replacement model scores better on public benchmarks. The system has a 600-case eval suite, and production prompts include several instructions written to correct the old model's habits. What is the soundest migration plan?
options: Switch the model ID in production on the retirement date, since the replacement scores better on public benchmarks and the prompts were already tested.
Run the evals on the replacement with current prompts, fix regressions and old-model workarounds, re-run, then roll out gradually with monitoring.
Ask the replacement model to rewrite the production prompts for itself, then deploy the rewritten prompts without running the eval suite, since the model knows what works for it.
Keep using the old model after retirement through a cached alias, which continues to point at the old version until the client chooses to move.
questions.explanation: A model migration is a change like any other: run your own evals, fix regressions (including prompt workarounds that no longer fit), and roll out in stages with monitoring (B). Public benchmarks (A) don't measure this client's prompts and cases. Model-rewritten prompts without evals (C) skip the gate that catches regressions. Retired models stop serving requests, and aliases move to newer versions (D).

questions.stem: A team is designing an experiment to test whether a new retrieval setup improves answer correctness for a support assistant. Baseline correctness is 82%. For each design choice, select Yes if it is sound experiment design.
statements: Decide the primary metric, the minimum effect worth detecting and the sample size before the experiment starts.
Check the results every morning and stop as soon as the new setup is ahead with p < 0.05.
Randomize by conversation rather than by message, so each conversation sees only one retrieval setup.
questions.explanation: Statement 1: Yes. Fixing the metric, minimum detectable effect and sample size in advance prevents choosing them after seeing the data. Statement 2: No. Stopping at the first significant result inflates false positives; run to the planned sample. Statement 3: Yes. The unit of randomization should match the unit of outcome, here the conversation.

questions.stem: A legal-research assistant's answers are graded by an LLM judge that checks 'Is the answer accurate and well-supported?' Scores have stayed near 92% for months, but attorneys report more wrong citations. Investigation shows the judge sees only the answer, not the retrieved sources. What should change in the evaluation?
options: Raise the judge's pass threshold from 'mostly accurate' to 'fully accurate,' which makes the judge stricter about citations without changing its inputs.
Replace the judge with a keyword check that confirms each answer contains at least one citation in the expected format, which is faster and fully deterministic.
Give the judge the retrieved sources, grade whether each cited passage supports its claim, and validate the judge against attorney labels.
Keep the judge as it is and add a monthly survey of attorneys, since user satisfaction is a better measure than automated grading.
questions.explanation: A judge can't check grounding without the sources. Give it the evidence, break the question into specific criteria, and confirm it agrees with expert labels (C). A stricter threshold (A) changes the bar but the judge still can't see whether citations are right. A format check (B) confirms citations exist, not that they support the claim. A survey (D) is slow and too coarse to catch specific citation errors.

questions.stem: An evaluation lead is choosing grading methods for an insurance assistant's eval suite. Match each check to the best grading method.
choices: Exact or programmatic check in code
LLM judge with a rubric, validated against expert labels
Human expert review of a sample
Production monitoring of a live metric
rows: Whether the extracted policy number matches the format and the value in the source document.
Whether the tone of a claim-denial letter is respectful and clear, across thousands of letters.
Whether a new kind of coverage advice, never seen before launch, is legally correct in the first weeks.
questions.explanation: Row 1: a field with one right value and a fixed format is best checked in code (A). Row 2: tone across thousands of letters is subjective but repetitive, which suits a rubric-based judge checked against expert labels (B). Row 3: novel, high-stakes legal correctness needs expert review until there is enough labeled data to automate (C). Live monitoring (D) tracks trends after launch but doesn't grade any of these individual checks.

questions.stem: A team's offline eval set for a travel assistant was built a year ago from launch-week conversations. Offline scores remain at 90%, but the share of conversations escalated to human agents has climbed from 8% to 15% over six months. The product now supports rail bookings, which didn't exist at launch. What does this most likely indicate, and what should the team do?
options: The eval set no longer reflects production; add labeled recent cases, especially rail bookings and escalations, and track scores by segment.
The escalation increase is a staffing issue in the human team, since offline scores show the assistant's quality hasn't changed.
The model has degraded over time, so the team should switch to a newer model and keep the existing eval set as the regression baseline.
The judge used for offline scoring has become more lenient over time, so the team should lower the passing threshold to match what the escalation data shows.
questions.explanation: Stable offline scores alongside worse production signals and a new feature point to an eval set that has drifted from real traffic. Refresh it from recent conversations and segment results (A). Blaming staffing (B) ignores that the assistant's escalation rate is what rose. Models behind a pinned ID don't degrade on their own (C). Changing the threshold (D) hides the gap instead of measuring the new traffic.

questions.stem: A team compares two prompts on 400 test cases. Prompt A is correct on 352 cases and prompt B on 360. They want to ship B. A reviewer asks whether the difference is real. The same 400 cases were run through both prompts. Which analysis answers the question best?
options: Compare the two accuracy figures directly: 90% is higher than 88% on the same 400 cases, so B is better.
Run each prompt once more and ship B if it wins again, since two wins in a row rule out chance.
Compute a separate confidence interval for each prompt's accuracy and ship B only if the two intervals don't overlap at all.
Use a paired comparison on the cases where the two prompts disagree, and estimate the uncertainty of the difference.
questions.explanation: Because both prompts ran on the same cases, a paired analysis focused on the cases where they disagree is the right test, and it is more sensitive than comparing two separate accuracies (D). Comparing raw figures (A) ignores uncertainty. Two wins in a row (B) is not a statistical test. Non-overlapping separate intervals (C) is overly conservative and ignores the pairing.

questions.stem: A team is reducing the cost of a high-volume document classifier that runs at the default effort level with a 6,000-token instruction block on every request. Evals show no quality difference at lower effort. For each optimization, select Yes if it is likely to reduce cost without hurting quality.
statements: Lower the effort level for this classifier, and keep checking quality on the eval set.
Cache the 6,000-token instruction block, with the breakpoint after the instructions and the document after it.
Ask the model to explain its reasoning in detail before every label, so that fewer labels need human correction later.
questions.explanation: Statement 1: Yes. Evals show lower effort keeps quality, and it reduces tokens and latency. Statement 2: Yes. A large, stable instruction block repeated on every request is the textbook case for prompt caching. Statement 3: No. Detailed reasoning on every label adds output tokens, which cost more than input tokens, without evidence of a quality gain on this task.

questions.stem: A support assistant's weekly quality review uses 50 randomly sampled conversations. The team wants to know whether a recent change hurt answers about refunds, which are 3% of traffic. In the last three weekly samples, only four refund conversations appeared in total. What should change in the review?
options: Increase the weekly sample from 50 to 100 conversations, which doubles the number of refund conversations that get reviewed each week by the team.
Stratify the sample: draw a fixed number of refund conversations each week on top of the random sample, and track refunds separately.
Stop reviewing refund conversations and rely on complaint volume, since refunds are too rare to sample meaningfully.
Ask the assistant to flag which of its own refund answers it is unsure about, and review only those conversations each week alongside the random sample.
questions.explanation: Rare but important segments need stratified sampling so each gets enough cases to measure, with results tracked per segment (B). Doubling a random sample (A) still yields only a handful of refund cases. Complaints (C) are a lagging, partial signal. The model's own uncertainty (D) is not a reliable selector for its errors.

questions.stem: An evaluation lead is choosing metrics for three Claude features. Match each feature to the most appropriate primary metric.
choices: Recall on the critical class, with precision tracked
Exact-match field accuracy against labeled documents
Rubric score from a validated LLM judge
Latency at p95
rows: A classifier that routes suspected fraud reports, where missing a real report is very costly.
An extraction step that pulls six fields from purchase orders into an ERP.
A drafting assistant whose replies must be accurate, polite and complete, across thousands of replies a week.
questions.explanation: Row 1: when misses are costly, recall on that class is the primary metric, with precision watched for reviewer load (A). Row 2: fields with one right value are measured by exact-match accuracy against labels (B). Row 3: open-ended quality at volume suits a rubric-based judge validated against human ratings (C). Latency (D) is a guardrail for all three, not the primary measure of whether any of them does its job.

questions.stem: A team is building the evaluation set for a new policy-question assistant before launch. For each practice, select Yes if it is sound.
statements: Include questions the policies don't answer, with the expected behavior being to say so and escalate.
Use the same examples in the prompt's few-shot section and in the evaluation set, since they are the best-reviewed examples available.
Version the evaluation set and record which version produced each reported score.
questions.explanation: Statement 1: Yes. Testing unanswerable questions checks that the assistant doesn't invent answers. Statement 2: No. Examples used in the prompt must be held out of the evaluation set, or scores overstate real performance. Statement 3: Yes. Versioning the set makes scores comparable over time and changes traceable.

questions.stem: A team wants to cut the cost of a Claude-based document assistant without hurting quality. Match each finding to the optimization it points to.
choices: Cache the long, stable instruction block
Route simple requests to a smaller model, confirmed on evals
Ask for shorter outputs that match what users read
Move the work to the Batches API
rows: Every request repeats the same 9,000-token instructions, and input tokens are most of the bill.
Users read only the first paragraph of summaries that average 700 words.
Seventy percent of requests are simple lookups that a smaller model handles as well on the eval set.
questions.explanation: Row 1: a large repeated prefix that dominates input cost is the case for prompt caching (A). Row 2: paying for 700 words when users read one paragraph points to shorter outputs, checked against quality (C). Row 3: a large share of simple requests that a smaller model handles equally well points to routing (B). Batch processing (D) suits work that can wait hours, and nothing here says these requests can.

questions.stem: A hospital network has signed Anthropic's BAA and enabled a HIPAA-ready API organization. The CIO says, 'We're covered, so the app is HIPAA compliant.' Which TWO statements correct this view?
options: Coverage is feature-specific, and data sent to third-party services sits outside the BAA.
The hospital must still meet HIPAA itself: access controls, audit logs, minimum-necessary use, and protection of PHI in its logs, caches and indexes.
The BAA extends to every Anthropic product the hospital's staff use, including individual plans, as long as they use work email addresses.
With a BAA in place, PHI can be included in any prompt or feature, since Anthropic is now contractually responsible for protecting it.
HIPAA applies to the hospital's records systems, not to AI processing services, so the BAA is a formality.
questions.explanation: Being HIPAA-eligible (the vendor will sign a BAA for specific services) is different from being compliant (your whole implementation meets the rules). Coverage is feature-specific, and the customer remains responsible for its own safeguards. Consumer plans cannot enable HIPAA coverage (C). PHI use still follows minimum-necessary rules (D). HIPAA applies regardless of technology (E).

questions.stem: An EU customer exercises the GDPR right to erasure against a support platform built on Claude. Which TWO locations must the erasure process cover?
options: Public help-center articles that were used as retrieval sources in the customer's conversations.
Logs, transcripts and cached responses that contain the customer's data.
The foundation model's weights, which must be retrained without the customer's data.
Aggregate dashboards that show ticket counts by category and month, without any customer identifiers.
Chunks and embeddings in the vector index derived from the customer's tickets and emails, including archived copies.
questions.explanation: Personal data spreads into derived stores. Erasure must cover logs, transcripts and caches that hold the customer's data (B), and the chunks and embeddings derived from their tickets, including archived copies (E), which is why chunks should carry source and subject identifiers. Aggregates with no identifiers (D) hold no personal data. Using a pretrained model through an API does not put your customer's data into its weights (C). Public pages that never held the data (A) are out of scope. Evaluation sets built from production conversations would also be in scope, and so are the provider's retention terms for API data.

questions.stem: A claims-triage feature sends full customer records (name, address, SSN, medical history and 40 other fields) to Claude, although the task only needs the incident description, policy type and claim amount. Which principle is violated, and what is the fix?
options: Fairness: remove the address and zip code fields, which can act as proxies for protected characteristics.
Transparency: add a notice to outputs stating which customer data was used to produce each triage decision.
Data minimization (minimum necessary): send only the fields the task needs and pseudonymize any required identifiers.
No principle is violated; the extra context improves accuracy and all fields are already in the insurer's own systems.
questions.explanation: GDPR's data minimization principle and HIPAA's minimum-necessary standard both require limiting personal data to what the purpose needs. Pseudonymization keeps references usable while reducing exposure. A disclaimer (B) does not reduce exposure. Removing one field (A) is incomplete. Extra fields add risk and can distract the model (D).

questions.stem: A federal agency program office wants a Claude-based document assistant. Its authorization to operate (ATO) covers workloads only within specific, FedRAMP-authorized cloud environments. What should drive the architecture first?
options: Procurement simplicity: start with individual subscriptions for the program office while the formal authorization process runs.
Governance constraints first: design only within Claude options authorized for the agency's environment.
Model capability: choose the highest-scoring model on public benchmarks, then work with the agency to extend the ATO to cover its hosting.
Speed to value: prototype on the public API with representative agency documents, then migrate to an authorized environment for production.
questions.explanation: Compliance requirements filter the option space before performance and cost trade-offs. An offering outside the authorized boundary is not an option, however capable it is. Benchmark-first selection (C), prototyping on unauthorized services with real data (D) and individual subscriptions outside a governed deployment (A) all risk violating the ATO.

questions.stem: A lender uses Claude to draft adverse-action rationale for declined small-business loans. Regulators require that declines be explainable and reviewed. What human-in-the-loop design is most appropriate?
options: Human review of a random 10% of declines, with the review rate increased if the error rate exceeds a threshold.
Human review whenever an applicant disputes a decline, with automatic reversal if the reviewer disagrees.
Claude drafts cited rationales; a credit officer approves every decline; overrides are logged.
Automated declines with the rationale emailed to applicants, plus a monthly compliance review of a risk-based sample.
questions.explanation: High-impact decisions affecting individuals call for mandatory human review, with grounded drafts that make review efficient and auditable, and logged overrides that improve the system. Full automation (D) and sampled or complaint-driven review (A, B) leave most adverse decisions without the required oversight.

questions.stem: A refund agent's system prompt says 'Never issue refunds above $500 without manager approval.' During testing, a user persuades the agent that 'the manager already approved it in another chat,' and a $900 refund goes through. What is the correct control?
options: Enforce the limit in the refund tool's code using the order's value from the system of record, routing $500 or more to an approval queue.
Add a verifier agent that reviews each refund decision against the policy before the tool is called.
Set temperature to 0 so the agent applies the policy deterministically and is less susceptible to persuasion.
Strengthen the prompt: state the limit in several places, add examples of manipulation attempts, and require the agent to quote the policy before refunding.
questions.explanation: Hard business rules belong in deterministic code at the point of action, using trusted data rather than model-supplied amounts or claims. Prompts guide behavior; they do not enforce it. Louder prompts (D), agent-on-agent checks (B) and temperature (C) are all still probabilistic.

questions.stem: An executive-assistant agent reads incoming email and can send email, schedule meetings and share documents. Security is concerned about prompt injection through inbound messages. Which TWO controls most reduce the risk of harmful actions?
options: Scope credentials and tools to the minimum needed, such as internal-only sharing.
Have the model classify each email as trustworthy or not, and follow embedded requests only from trustworthy senders.
Add a detailed catalog of known injection techniques to the system prompt so the model recognizes them.
Require explicit user confirmation for outbound or irreversible actions, showing the exact action before it runs.
Turn off logging of email content, so injected instructions are not retained or replayed.
questions.explanation: Assume some injections will succeed and limit the damage: human confirmation for consequential actions and least-privilege capabilities. Model-based trust classification (B) can itself be manipulated. Long lists of known attacks (C) miss new ones. Disabling logging (E) removes detection and audit.

questions.stem: A recruiting team wants Claude to shortlist applicants. They propose removing name, gender and age fields from résumés to make it fair. Which TWO points should you raise?
options: Removing protected attributes does not ensure fairness, because proxies such as schools, graduation years or zip codes correlate with protected groups.
Higher temperature reduces systematic bias by introducing randomness into which candidates are shortlisted.
Shortlisting is advisory and humans make the final hire, so fairness obligations apply only at the hiring decision.
With protected fields removed, the model cannot discriminate, so a one-time check at launch is sufficient.
Measure outcomes: compare shortlisting rates across groups on a representative test set and in production, with humans accountable.
questions.explanation: Blinding inputs is insufficient because of proxy variables. Fairness has to be measured on outcomes and governed with human accountability. Shortlisting is a consequential decision that shapes who is considered (C). Randomness (B) is not fairness. Skipping evaluation (D) leaves bias undetected.

questions.stem: A public benefits portal will deploy a Claude assistant to help residents understand eligibility. Which transparency practice is most important?
options: Keep answers short by omitting sources, since residents mainly want a quick yes or no on eligibility.
Disclose AI involvement in the portal's terms of service, which residents accept when creating an account.
Disclose clearly that residents are using AI, show the policy sources behind answers and the assistant's limits, and offer a path to a caseworker.
Give the assistant a friendly human name and persona so residents feel comfortable, while noting AI use in the privacy policy.
questions.explanation: Transparency means people know they are dealing with AI, can see where answers come from, understand what the system can and cannot do, and can reach a human. Impersonating a human (D) is deceptive. Hiding sources (A) or burying the disclosure (B) undermines informed use.

questions.stem: An internal legal-research assistant sometimes returns plausible but nonexistent case citations. Lawyers have nearly filed one. Which mitigation directly targets this failure mode?
options: Limit answers to a short summary without citations, so there are no citations to fabricate.
Ground answers in a verified corpus with citations, validate them, and require attorney sign-off.
Use a lower temperature and a more capable model, which together sharply reduce fabricated citations.
Strengthen the system prompt to require citing only real cases with full reporter citations, and to say when unsure.
questions.explanation: Fabricated citations are a known failure mode. Grounding in provided documents, structured citations that point only to supplied sources, programmatic checks and human verification together address it. Prompt instructions (D) and model or temperature changes (C) reduce but do not prevent fabrication. Dropping citations (A) removes the lawyers' means of verification.

questions.stem: A consumer chat app streams Claude's answers word by word for responsiveness. A policy classifier runs in parallel on the user's input, but harmful content occasionally reaches the screen before the classifier flags the request. What is the correct design?
options: Run the classifier on the complete answer after it is displayed, and retract the message if it is flagged.
Buffer streamed output until the fast classifier passes, and add output screening.
Turn off streaming and return answers only after the input classifier has finished, accepting the added latency.
Add a report button, so users can flag harmful content for removal and review.
questions.explanation: Parallel guardrails save latency only if the release of output is gated on their verdict. Output screening catches harmful answers to innocuous-looking requests. Dropping streaming (C) gives up responsiveness unnecessarily. Post-display checks (A) and user reports (D) come too late.

questions.stem: To reduce cost, a team caches final answers keyed by normalized question text. Executives and staff use the same assistant, and some answers draw on executive-only compensation documents. What is the risk, and what is the fix?
options: Encrypt the cache at rest and in transit, so cached executive answers are protected.
Answers built from restricted documents can be served to unauthorized users; include the permission scope in the cache key.
Shorten cache expiry to one minute, so a restricted answer is unlikely to be requested by someone else in that window.
No risk: the cache stores only final answers, not the restricted source documents themselves.
questions.explanation: An answer derived from restricted data is itself restricted. Caches must respect authorization boundaries and be invalidated when content or permissions change. A short TTL (C) narrows the window but does not close it. Encryption (A) protects data at rest but does not stop it being served to the wrong user. Caching only final answers (D) doesn't remove the risk: the answer itself contains the restricted information.

questions.stem: A security team wants to prevent Claude Code from reading .env files and secrets across all developer machines in the organization. Which TWO controls provide the strongest enforcement?
options: Developer training on not pasting secrets into prompts, with a signed acknowledgment.
Enable sandboxing through managed settings, with OS-level filesystem read restrictions on secret paths.
A line in each repository's CLAUDE.md telling Claude not to read .env files or secrets.
A deny rule for .env in each developer's user settings, set up during onboarding.
Managed deny rules for secret paths, with bypass mode disabled.
questions.explanation: Managed deny rules are the organization-wide permission layer and take precedence over user and project settings. Disabling bypass mode prevents a developer from turning off all checks. Because permission rules act on Claude Code's tools and recognized commands, while a script could still open a file, OS-level sandboxing closes the remaining gap. CLAUDE.md (C) is guidance, not enforcement. User settings (D) can be changed by the user. Training (A) is not a technical control.

questions.stem: A public-facing assistant is being targeted by users trying to jailbreak it into producing prohibited content and to extract its system prompt. Which TWO measures form the strongest layered defense?
options: Screen inputs and outputs with classifiers, gating what is displayed, and log flagged attempts.
Rely on the model's built-in safety training, which is designed to resist jailbreaks and prompt extraction.
Put a confidential instruction in the system prompt telling the model not to reveal its prompt or discuss its rules with users.
Raise the temperature so responses vary and attackers cannot iterate toward a working jailbreak.
Application-layer abuse controls: rate limits, per-account anomaly monitoring, and blocking of repeat offenders.
questions.explanation: Effective defenses combine content-level screening with platform-level abuse controls. Built-in model safety is a valuable layer but not the only one (B). Secrets in prompts (C) are a target, not a defense. Temperature (D) does not improve safety.

questions.stem: An HR assistant drafts responses to employee relations cases, some involving discipline and termination recommendations. Leadership wants to auto-send drafts to save time. What is the appropriate governance decision?
options: Do not use AI for employee relations at all, because any error carries legal risk.
Auto-send all drafts with an 'AI-generated' label, so employees know to verify the content themselves.
Auto-send all drafts, since testing showed high accuracy and HR can correct any issue afterwards.
Tier by impact: automate low-risk answers; require HR approval for discipline and termination.
questions.explanation: Human oversight should scale with impact. Decisions with significant effects on individuals need review and accountability, while low-risk content can be automated with monitoring. All-or-nothing approaches (A, C) either over-automate or forgo safe value. A label (B) does not provide oversight.

questions.stem: An EU insurer requires that personal data be processed in the EU. The team deploys Claude through Amazon Bedrock and selects the global endpoint for best availability. What is the issue?
options: A global endpoint may route across regions; use in-region inference in the EU instead.
Nothing: Bedrock processes requests in the region where the API is called, regardless of endpoint type.
Use the global endpoint but encrypt requests, which keeps the data under EU jurisdiction.
Residency rules cover where data is stored, not where it is processed, so the endpoint choice does not matter.
questions.explanation: Endpoint choice affects where inference runs. Bedrock offers both global (cross-region routing) and in-region options, and residency rules usually concern processing, not only storage (D). Bedrock does not always process in the calling region (B). Encryption (C) protects data in transit but does not change where it is processed.

questions.stem: A team plans to use Claude to summarize employee performance reviews. A privacy officer asks what failure modes and limitations must be documented before approval. Which response is most complete?
options: 'We will monitor employee complaints after launch and address issues as they arise.'
'Testing showed high accuracy, so there are no material limitations to document beyond normal software risk.'
Document each known failure mode, the control that mitigates it, the residual risk, and the escalation path.
'Model errors are covered by the vendor's terms, so liability for limitations rests with the vendor.'
questions.explanation: Governance requires an honest inventory of risks with a mitigating control for each and acknowledged residual risk. Claims of no limitations (B), purely reactive monitoring (A) and shifting responsibility to the vendor (D) do not meet that standard.

questions.stem: A shared Claude Code configuration allows developers to run the agent in bypass-permissions mode for speed. A security review flags that this turns off all permission checks. What organizational control addresses this?
options: Uninstall Claude Code from developer machines until a safer configuration is available.
Publish a policy asking developers not to use bypass mode, and review compliance quarterly.
Reset each developer's local settings file weekly through a scheduled script.
Disable bypass mode in managed settings and use managed allow rules for speed.
questions.explanation: Managed settings are the enforcement layer that users cannot override, and Claude Code's documentation provides a specific setting to disable bypass mode. Speed can be preserved with deliberate allow rules rather than disabling all checks. Requests (B) are not controls. Removal (A) and deleting files (C) are blunt or easily circumvented.

questions.stem: An agent will be allowed to modify production data (closing tickets, updating CRM fields, issuing credits). Which TWO risk controls are most important to design in from the start?
options: A reversible audit trail of every action, with model and prompt versions.
Have the model assess each action's risk and request approval when it judges an action risky.
Broad database credentials matching the DBA team's, so the agent doesn't fail partway through for lack of permissions.
Unlimited automatic retries on failed writes, so transient errors don't leave work half done.
Tiered autonomy: low-impact reversible actions run automatically, while high-impact actions need human approval enforced in code.
questions.explanation: Autonomy should match risk and be enforced deterministically, and every action should be auditable and reversible. Unlimited retries (D) risk duplicate side effects. Broad credentials (C) violate least privilege. Model self-judgment (B) is not an enforcement mechanism.

questions.stem: A clinic wants to summarize visit notes with Claude while minimizing PHI exposure, and asks whether de-identifying the notes first means HIPAA no longer applies to the pipeline. What is the most accurate answer?
options: Yes: removing patient names and medical record numbers is enough to de-identify clinical notes.
Only if it meets Safe Harbor or Expert Determination; free text often hides identifiers.
No: HIPAA applies to all medical text, even when fully de-identified, so de-identification has no effect.
Yes, as long as the model is instructed not to retain or repeat any personal information.
questions.explanation: Properly de-identified data is not PHI, but the bar is specific, and clinical free text routinely contains identifiers beyond names (dates, locations, relatives, record numbers). Removing names alone (A) does not meet the standard. De-identified data is not restricted by the Privacy Rule (C). Instructions to the model (D) are irrelevant to the legal status of the data.

questions.stem: A bank's loan-servicing agent reads account data and can send payment reminders. Regulators may ask, months later, why a specific customer got a specific message. Which TWO things must the audit log record for each agent action?
options: The exact model ID and prompt version used, plus the inputs and retrieved documents the model saw.
Every tool call with its arguments and result, and who approved it if approval was required.
A daily summary of how many messages were sent, grouped by message type and region.
The model's confidence score for each message, so reviewers can sort messages by risk.
A screenshot of the customer's account page taken at the moment the message was sent.
questions.explanation: To explain one decision later, you need to know exactly what the model was and what it saw (A), and exactly what it did and who signed off (B). A daily count can't explain a single message (C). Claude doesn't return a calibrated confidence score, and a score wouldn't explain the decision anyway (D). A screenshot is unstructured and misses the prompt, model and tool calls (E).

questions.stem: A team connects a free third-party MCP server that offers a 'format_date' tool. Later they find its tool description contains hidden text telling Claude to send the contents of any file it reads to an outside URL. What is the most effective control going forward?
options: Add a line to the system prompt telling Claude to ignore instructions found inside tool descriptions.
Only allow MCP servers that have been reviewed and approved, pinned to a reviewed version.
Turn on extended thinking so Claude reasons more carefully before following tool descriptions.
Keep the server but rename its tools so their names no longer match the hidden instructions.
questions.explanation: Tool descriptions go straight into the model's context, so a malicious server can inject instructions. The fix is to control which servers are allowed at all and pin reviewed versions, so a later update can't slip new text in (B). A prompt line is a soft defense that injected text can work around (A). Extended thinking doesn't make the model immune to instructions it's given (C). Renaming tools doesn't remove the hidden text (D).

questions.stem: A developer puts the company's payment-API key in the system prompt so Claude can 'call the API when needed.' A user then asks the assistant to repeat its instructions word for word. What is the correct design?
options: Keep the key in the prompt, but tell Claude not to reveal it under any circumstances, and test that it refuses to.
Encrypt the key inside the prompt text so it can't be read even if it is repeated back.
Keep the key on the server; Claude calls a tool, and the tool's code adds the key to the request.
Rotate the key every day so that any copy a user extracts expires quickly.
questions.explanation: Anything in the context can end up in the output, so secrets must never be in the prompt. The tool's server-side code should attach credentials, and the model only ever sees the tool name and arguments (C). A 'never reveal' instruction can be talked around (A). An encrypted key Claude can't decrypt is useless, and one it can decrypt is still exposed (B). Daily rotation shortens the exposure but still leaks the key (D).

questions.stem: A team logs every full prompt and response to its logging platform for debugging. A review finds the logs contain customer Social Security numbers and medical details, and 60 engineers can search them. What is the best fix?
options: Stop logging prompts and responses, and debug from the reports and screenshots that users send in instead.
Redact sensitive fields before logs are written, restrict access, and set a retention limit.
Move the logs to a different logging vendor that offers better encryption at rest.
Ask engineers to sign an acknowledgment that they won't search the logs for customers' personal data.
questions.explanation: Logs are a second copy of sensitive data and need the same protection: mask sensitive fields before they're stored, limit who can read them, and delete them on a schedule (B). Dropping all logging removes the ability to investigate problems and to audit (A). Better encryption at rest doesn't stop 60 people from searching the data (C). An acknowledgment is a policy, not a control (D).

questions.stem: A database agent answers analysts' questions by writing SQL. It currently connects with the same credentials the application uses, which can insert, update and delete rows. What is the most important change?
options: Add 'only write SELECT statements' to the system prompt, with examples of safe queries.
Have the code reject any query containing the words UPDATE, DELETE or DROP before it runs.
Give the agent a separate read-only database role that can see only the tables it needs.
Log every query the agent runs and review the log every week for anything that changed data.
questions.explanation: Least privilege at the database is the control that can't be bypassed: a read-only role limited to the needed tables makes a damaging query impossible (C). A prompt instruction is soft (A). Keyword filtering can be bypassed (for example, through stored procedures or odd formatting) and is fragile (B). A weekly review finds damage after it's done (D).

questions.stem: A nursing assistant tool suggests medication dose adjustments. The plan is to send suggestions straight into the patient chart and have a pharmacist review a 10% random sample each week. What should change?
options: Raise the weekly review sample from 10% to 50%, so more mistakes are caught each week.
Require a pharmacist to approve each suggestion before it reaches the patient chart.
Add a disclaimer to each suggestion saying it was generated by AI and may be wrong.
Use a larger model for dose suggestions, since bigger models make fewer arithmetic errors.
questions.explanation: A wrong dose can cause serious harm that can't be undone, so the human check has to come before the action, not after (B). Sampling after the fact, at any rate, still lets errors reach patients (A). A disclaimer doesn't stop a wrong dose being given (C). A bigger model lowers the error rate but doesn't remove it (D).

questions.stem: A lender uses Claude to help triage loan applications. Six months later, an applicant appeals a decision. The team can see the final decision but not what the model was given or which prompt was live that day. What should have been designed in?
options: Re-running the application through today's prompt and model, and showing the result to the reviewer.
Storing, for each decision, the inputs sent, the model ID, the prompt version and the raw output.
Asking the model to write a longer explanation, so the reasoning in the decision letter is clearer.
Setting temperature to 0, so that re-running the same application will reproduce the decision.
questions.explanation: An appeal needs a record of what actually happened at the time: the inputs, the model version, the prompt version and the output (B). Today's prompt and model may give a different answer (A). A longer explanation doesn't record what the system saw (C). Temperature 0 doesn't guarantee an identical rerun, and the model or prompt may have changed since (D).

questions.stem: A customer-facing assistant goes live next month. The team wants to red-team it. Which TWO practices make the red-teaming most useful?
options: Include attacks hidden in the documents and web pages the assistant reads, not only in what users type.
Turn the successful attacks into an eval set and re-run it whenever the prompt or model changes.
Run red-teaming once before launch, since attacks that failed then will keep failing afterward.
Limit testing to the exact phrasings in public jailbreak lists, so the results are easy to compare.
Have only the developers who wrote the prompt do the testing, since they know its weak points best.
questions.explanation: Indirect injection through retrieved content is a major attack path and must be tested (A). Saving successful attacks as regression tests catches weaknesses that come back after a prompt or model change (B). A single pre-launch test misses regressions (C). Public phrasings are a narrow slice of real attacks (D). The people who wrote the prompt have blind spots, so independent testers find more (E).

questions.stem: On a Friday afternoon, a user reports that the support assistant showed them another customer's order history. What should happen first?
options: Ask the model in a test chat why it showed the wrong customer's data, and log its answer.
Turn off the affected feature with a kill switch, keep the logs, and start the incident process.
Add a rule to the system prompt saying not to show one customer's data to another customer, then keep monitoring.
Wait for a second report before acting, since one report could be a misunderstanding.
questions.explanation: A possible data leak means stop the harm first: disable the feature, preserve the evidence, and follow the incident and notification process (B). The model can't reliably explain its own past behavior (A). A prompt rule doesn't fix what is likely a session, cache or authorization bug in the code (C). Waiting lets more customers' data leak (D).

questions.stem: An EU retailer runs Claude in an EU region to keep personal data in the EU. Its observability tool sends every prompt and response to a monitoring service hosted in the US. What is the problem?
options: None: data residency only applies to where the model runs, not to where logs are stored.
The prompts and responses contain personal data, so the logs leave the EU and break the requirement.
The only problem is cost, since sending every log record abroad adds bandwidth charges for each request.
Monitoring tools can't read Claude responses, so the US service receives only empty records.
questions.explanation: Data residency covers every copy of the data, including logs, traces and analytics. If prompts contain customer data, shipping them to a US service moves that data out of the EU (B). Residency isn't limited to where the model runs (A). Cost isn't the issue (C). Monitoring tools receive whatever the application sends them, which here is the full text (D).

questions.stem: An agent can read a user's email and send replies on their behalf. Which TWO controls best limit the damage if an incoming email contains hidden instructions?
options: Require the user to confirm before any email is sent, showing the recipient and full text.
Restrict sending to people the user has emailed before, enforced in the tool's code.
Tell the model in the system prompt that emails may contain instructions it should ignore.
Strip all formatting and links from incoming emails before the model reads them.
Switch to a smaller model for reading email, since it follows hidden instructions less often.
questions.explanation: A user confirmation step (A) and a recipient limit enforced in code (B) both hold even if the model is fooled, because they control the action, not the model's judgment. A warning in the prompt is a soft defense (C). Stripping formatting doesn't remove plain-text instructions (D). Model size isn't a security control (E).

questions.stem: A product manager wants a quick way to stop the AI assistant if it starts giving harmful answers on a weekend, without waiting for a code deployment. What should be built in from the start?
options: A feature flag that switches users to a fallback (human queue or static help) within minutes.
An on-call engineer who can edit the system prompt directly in production when needed.
A daily batch job that reviews the previous day's answers and emails a report on Monday.
A setting that lowers the temperature to 0, so that harmful answers become less likely.
questions.explanation: A kill switch with a safe fallback lets anyone authorized stop the harm immediately, without a deployment (A). Editing prompts live in production is risky and untested, and it may not stop the problem (B). A daily report finds the problem too late (C). Lower temperature doesn't stop harmful answers (D).

questions.stem: A startup is building a consumer app that gives people personalized advice about their health insurance claims. Under Anthropic's Usage Policy, what extra requirements apply to this kind of high-risk, consumer-facing use?
options: None, as long as the app has a privacy policy and terms of service.
Qualified human review of the advice before it's relied on, and telling users that AI is involved.
Only a requirement to use the most capable Claude model for every answer.
A ban on all insurance-related use, since insurance advice is one of the categories the Usage Policy prohibits for any purpose.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's Usage Policy treats consumer-facing advice in areas such as healthcare, insurance, legal and finance as high-risk. Those uses require a qualified human in the loop and disclosure that AI is being used (B). A privacy policy alone isn't enough (A). Model choice isn't the requirement (C). Insurance use isn't banned (D).

questions.stem: A company's legal team asks whether prompts and outputs sent through the commercial Claude API will be used to train Anthropic's models. What is the accurate starting point?
options: Yes, all API traffic is used for training unless the company pays for a premium plan.
Under the commercial terms, inputs and outputs aren't used for training by default; confirm the details in the contract.
Only outputs are used for training; inputs are discarded once the response has been returned.
It depends on the model chosen; smaller models are trained on customer data.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's commercial terms say customer API data isn't used to train models by default. The legal team should still confirm retention and use terms in the actual agreement (B). There's no pay-to-opt-out arrangement (A). Inputs and outputs aren't treated differently in that way (C), and it doesn't depend on model size (D).

questions.stem: A hiring team wants to check whether its résumé-screening assistant treats candidates fairly. Which test is most informative?
options: Ask the model whether it is biased, and record its answer in the compliance file.
Run the same résumés with only the name or other group signals changed, and compare the outcomes.
Remove names from résumés and assume the outcomes are fair from then on.
Check that the assistant's overall pass rate is close to the human screening team's historical pass rate for the same roles.
questions.explanation: Counterfactual tests, with identical résumés where only group signals such as names differ, show directly whether those signals change the outcome (B). The model can't reliably report its own bias (A). Removing names doesn't remove other signals, such as schools or clubs (C). Matching the historical rate can copy past bias (D).

questions.stem: An agent writes code changes for a payments service. The team wants to prevent a single faulty or manipulated run from reaching production. Which TWO controls matter most?
options: The agent can't approve or merge its own changes; a person must review and approve them.
Production deployment requires the normal pipeline checks and can't be triggered by the agent directly.
The agent is told in its prompt to be extra careful with payment code.
The agent writes longer commit messages, so reviewers understand its changes.
The agent runs on a faster model, so changes are finished before the end of the day.
questions.explanation: Separation of duties means the agent that writes the change can't also approve it (A) or push it to production on its own (B). Both hold even if the agent is wrong or manipulated. A prompt request (C), better commit messages (D) or speed (E) don't stop a bad change.

questions.stem: A public chatbot is free to use. One user writes a script that sends 50,000 long requests in an hour, running up a large API bill. What control prevents this?
options: A notice in the terms of service saying that automated use is not allowed.
Per-user and per-IP rate limits and spending caps, enforced in the app's backend.
A longer system prompt telling the model to refuse any requests that look like they come from a script.
Raising the account's API spending limit, so that the service keeps running for everyone.
questions.explanation: Abuse that runs up costs, sometimes called denial of wallet, is stopped with limits enforced in code: requests and tokens per user or IP, plus spending caps (B). Terms of service don't stop a script (A). The model can't reliably spot automation, and every request still costs money (C). A higher limit makes the bill bigger (D).

questions.stem: A community forum uses Claude to draft replies to user posts. Some posts contain hate speech or illegal content. What is a sensible first line of defense?
options: Let Claude draft replies to everything, since it will refuse on its own to repeat any harmful content it sees.
Screen incoming posts with a fast, inexpensive classifier, and route flagged posts to moderators.
Delete any post longer than 500 words, since long posts are more likely to be harmful.
Block all posts that contain any negative words, such as 'hate' or 'kill.'
questions.explanation: A quick, cheap screening step catches problem content before it reaches the main workflow and sends it to people who can handle it properly (B). Relying on the drafting model alone mixes jobs and leaves gaps (A). Length isn't a signal of harm (C). Keyword blocking catches harmless posts and misses disguised ones (D).

questions.stem: A consultancy wants to send its clients' customer data to Claude to generate analysis. What must be in place before any client data is sent?
options: Nothing, since the consultancy already has the data on its own servers.
The client's contract must allow sharing with this processor, with the right data-processing terms in place.
A note in the consultancy's own privacy policy saying that AI tools may be used.
Encryption of the data at rest on the consultancy's laptops.
questions.explanation: Holding a client's data doesn't mean you may share it with another processor. The client agreement must permit it, with appropriate data-processing terms covering the provider (B). Possession isn't permission (A). The consultancy's own policy doesn't bind its clients' data (C). Encryption at rest doesn't address the sharing (D).

questions.stem: A support assistant stores every conversation forever 'in case it's useful later.' Conversations include addresses, order details and sometimes health information. What should the team set up?
options: Keep everything forever, but encrypt the storage so the data is protected.
A retention policy with a defined period by data type, automatic deletion, and a way to handle deletion requests.
Delete all conversations immediately, so that nothing at all is ever stored.
Move old conversations to a cheaper storage system after one year.
questions.explanation: Keep data only as long as there's a reason, with periods set by data type, automatic deletion, and a process for people's deletion requests (B). Encryption protects data but doesn't limit how long you hold it (A). Deleting immediately removes what's needed for support, audits and evals (C). Cheaper storage is still storage (D).

questions.stem: A bank requires a full review board meeting for every change to its AI systems. Simple wording fixes now take six weeks, so teams avoid making small improvements. What is a better governance approach?
options: Remove the review board, so that teams can ship any change immediately.
Tier changes by risk: low-risk edits pass automated eval gates, and high-risk changes go to the board.
Keep the board, and have it meet daily instead of weekly.
Freeze the AI systems until the board can clear its backlog, so that no unreviewed change reaches production.
questions.explanation: Risk-based tiering puts heavy review where it matters, such as changes to decision logic, tools or data access, while routine edits move quickly with automated checks (B). Removing the board removes oversight (A). Daily meetings add cost without fixing the bottleneck (C). Freezing stops needed fixes (D).

questions.stem: A company is planning eight AI use cases, from an internal meeting-notes summarizer to an assistant that recommends loan approvals. How should it decide how much governance each one needs?
options: Apply the strictest controls to all eight, so that none of them is under-protected.
Rate each by impact: who's affected, how severe a mistake would be, and whether it's reversible, then scale controls.
