Apply the same light controls to all eight, since they all use the same model.
Let each project team decide on its own controls, without any central guidance.
questions.explanation: A risk assessment by impact, such as affected people, harm if wrong, reversibility and regulation, lets controls match the stakes. The loan recommender gets far more than the notes summarizer (B). Maximum controls everywhere waste effort and slow low-risk work (A). The same model doesn't mean the same risk (C). No guidance leads to uneven protection (D).

questions.stem: An insurer uses Claude to help decide which claims to deny. Regulations give customers the right to challenge automated decisions. What must the design include?
options: A notice that decisions are final and can't be challenged once they are made.
A way for customers to request human review, with a reviewer who can see the case and change the decision.
An option for the customer to ask the AI to reconsider its own decision.
A rule that only claims under $1,000 can be denied with AI involved.
questions.explanation: Contesting an automated decision means a person with real authority reviews it, with access to the case facts and the system's inputs and output (B). Final decisions with no appeal break the requirement (A). Asking the same AI to reconsider isn't human review (C). An arbitrary amount doesn't satisfy the right to challenge (D).

questions.stem: An audit finds employees pasting confidential contract text into personal AI chat accounts to summarize it faster. What response best reduces this risk?
options: Send an email to all staff reminding them that confidential client data must not be pasted into any AI tool, personal or otherwise.
Provide an approved enterprise AI tool with proper data terms, plus a clear policy and data-loss controls.
Block all AI websites on the company network, including any approved enterprise tools.
Ask employees to remove client names before pasting text into personal accounts.
questions.explanation: People turn to unapproved tools when they lack approved ones. A sanctioned tool with the right data protections, a clear policy and technical controls removes the need and catches leaks (B). A reminder alone rarely changes behavior (A). Blocking everything pushes use to personal phones (C). Removing names still leaks confidential content (D).

questions.stem: An enterprise is rolling out Claude to 5,000 employees. Which TWO administrative controls matter most for security and oversight?
options: Sign-in through the company's identity provider, with accounts added and removed automatically.
Admin audit logs and usage reports, so the security team can review access and activity.
Letting each employee create their own account with a personal email address.
Sharing one admin account among the IT team, so access isn't blocked when someone is away.
Turning off logging, so that employee privacy is protected.
questions.explanation: Single sign-on with automatic provisioning and removal ensures only current employees have access (A). Audit logs and usage reports give the oversight security needs (B). Personal accounts escape company control (C). A shared admin account hides who did what (D). No logging removes oversight entirely (E).

questions.stem: A compliance lead has listed obligations for a Claude-based claims assistant. Match each obligation to the architecture control that best implements it.
choices: Field-level redaction before logs are written, plus a retention limit
Human approval enforced in code for decisions above a threshold
An audit trail of each decision with model ID, prompt version and sources
Routing data only through a deployment option approved for the required region
rows: Regulators may ask why a specific claim was denied two years ago.
Customer data must not be processed outside the EU.
Support logs must not keep customers' bank details longer than necessary.
questions.explanation: Row 1: explaining a past decision needs a durable audit trail of what ran and what it relied on (C). Row 2: a residency duty is met by the deployment route that keeps processing in the region, including logs and other copies (D). Row 3: data minimization in logs is met by redaction before writing plus a retention limit (A). Human approval (B) is the control for high-impact decisions, which none of these three obligations names.

questions.stem: A threat review lists four prompt-injection entry points for an email-triage agent that can read the inbox, search the CRM, draft replies and send emails. Which entry point should be ranked highest risk, and why?
options: The user's own chat messages to the agent, because the user can type any instruction they like into the chat window, including ones that override the rules.
The CRM's account notes, because sales staff write them by hand and they sometimes contain informal language.
Incoming emails from outside the company: attackers control their content, and the agent can act on it by sending email.
The system prompt, because it is the longest piece of text the agent reads and contains the most instructions.
questions.explanation: Rank by attacker control combined with what the agent can do afterwards: external emails are written by anyone, and the agent can send email, which creates an exfiltration path (C). The authenticated user (A) is the principal the agent serves, so their instructions aren't an injection. CRM notes (B) are internal and lower risk, though still data. The system prompt (D) is written by the developer, not an attacker.

questions.stem: A bank is deploying an agent that can read customer accounts and draft account-change requests. The security architect is reviewing controls for prompt injection through documents customers upload. For each control, select Yes if it meaningfully reduces the risk.
statements: Give the agent's tools the narrowest permissions the task needs, for example drafting changes but not executing them.
Rely on a line in the system prompt telling the model that uploaded documents can't contain instructions.
Require a human to approve any account change the agent drafts after reading an uploaded document.
questions.explanation: Statement 1: Yes. Least privilege limits what a successful injection can do. Statement 2: No. A prompt line can be a useful extra layer, but relying on it as the control leaves the risk in place. Statement 3: Yes. Human approval for high-impact actions after untrusted input breaks the path from injection to harm.

questions.stem: A recruiting firm uses Claude to rank applicants' résumés for interview. An audit of 2,000 rankings finds that applicants from two universities are ranked lower than others with similar experience. The firm's leadership asks what to do before the next hiring cycle in six weeks. What is the most responsible plan?
options: Remove university names from résumés before ranking and continue the next cycle as planned, since the names were the only signal that could have caused the gap.
Add an instruction telling the model to treat all universities equally, then re-run the same 2,000 résumés and confirm that the ranking gap has narrowed.
Stop using AI in hiring permanently, since any measured disparity means the system can't be used fairly.
Pause automated ranking, investigate likely proxies, test fixes on a held-out set with fairness metrics, and keep human review until the fix holds.
questions.explanation: Responsible handling of measured bias is to limit harm now, find the cause (which may be proxies beyond the name), test a fix with fairness metrics on held-out data, and keep human oversight until it holds (D). Removing names (A) may miss proxies such as location or clubs. An instruction (B) is unverified mitigation, and re-running the same 2,000 résumés isn't a held-out test. A permanent stop (C) skips the investigation that would show whether the system can be fixed.

questions.stem: A health-tech startup wants to run patient-intake summarization on Claude Managed Agents because it wants the hosted sandbox and session management. Its contracts require zero data retention with model providers. What should the architect flag?
options: Nothing: Managed Agents is part of the Claude API, so the organization's existing zero data retention arrangement applies to it automatically as well.
Sessions store history and outputs server-side, and Managed Agents isn't eligible for zero data retention, so this needs a different runtime.
Zero data retention only matters for training, and the commercial terms already say that API inputs aren't used for training by default.
The startup can meet the requirement by deleting each session right after it finishes, which is the same as zero data retention.
questions.explanation: Managed Agents is stateful by design, storing transcripts and sandbox state until they are deleted, and it isn't eligible for zero data retention, so a ZDR-bound workload needs a different runtime (B). Assuming the arrangement extends automatically (A) is the trap. Retention and training are separate questions (C). Deleting after use (D) is not the same contractual commitment as never retaining the data.

questions.stem: An internal agent has read access to a company wiki and write access to the ticketing system. A red team shows that a wiki page edited by any employee can make the agent close unrelated tickets. Closing tickets is reversible but disrupts on-call teams. Which mitigation set is most proportionate?
options: Remove the agent's write access entirely, since any agent that reads employee-editable content can't be allowed to change anything.
Retrain the employees who edit wiki pages, so they understand that the agent reads their pages and that text they paste in could cause problems for on-call teams.
Treat wiki content as untrusted, limit the close action to the requester's own tickets, log every action, and confirm bulk changes.
Add an instruction to the system prompt telling the agent to close only tickets that the user explicitly names in their request.
questions.explanation: Controls should match the harm: scope the action to the requester's tickets in code, keep an audit log, and add confirmation where the blast radius is large (C). Removing write access (A) gives up useful, reversible work when the risk can be bounded. Training editors (B) doesn't stop a malicious editor. A prompt instruction (D) is the kind of control the red team already bypassed.

questions.stem: A public-sector agency is preparing a risk register for a Claude-based assistant that helps residents apply for benefits. For each entry, select Yes if it is a well-formed risk entry for this register.
statements: The assistant may give wrong eligibility guidance; likelihood medium, impact high; controls: answers cite the official rule, evals by caseworkers, escalation link; owner: benefits program lead.
AI is risky; likelihood high; control: be careful when using it.
Residents may share more personal data than needed; controls: input guidance, redaction before logging, 30-day log retention; owner: data protection officer; reviewed quarterly.
questions.explanation: Statement 1: Yes. It names a specific harm, rates it, lists concrete controls and assigns an owner. Statement 2: No. It names no specific harm, has no measurable control and no owner, so nobody can act on it. Statement 3: Yes. It is specific, has concrete controls, an owner and a review cadence.

questions.stem: A team plans to let Claude generate SQL against the production analytics warehouse for business users. The warehouse contains salary data in two tables that only HR may query. The proposal enforces this by telling the model in the system prompt not to query the salary tables. What should the architect require instead?
options: Run queries under each user's own database role, or a role without access to the salary tables, so the database enforces the rule.
Keep the system-prompt rule but scan generated SQL for the two table names and block queries that mention them before they run.
Train business users not to ask salary questions, and review the query log every month for any requests that touched the two salary tables.
Remove the salary tables from the schema description given to the model, so the model doesn't know the tables exist and can't write queries against them.
questions.explanation: Authorization must be enforced by the system that holds the data, so run queries under roles that can't read the restricted tables (A). Name matching (B) is bypassed by views, aliases or joins. Training and log review (C) detect misuse after the fact. Hiding tables from the model (D) is obscurity; a crafted query can still reach them.

questions.stem: An engineering org allows Claude Code across 300 repositories. Security asks how to keep secrets such as .env files and cloud credentials out of the model's reach, consistently, without relying on each engineer's configuration. Which approach meets the requirement?
options: Ask every engineer to add deny rules for secret files to their personal user settings, and have security check a sample of laptops each quarter for compliance.
Add a line to each repository's CLAUDE.md telling Claude not to open files that contain secrets or credentials.
Deploy deny rules for secret paths through managed settings, which override user and project settings and apply in every mode.
Run Claude Code only in plan mode across the organization, since plan mode can read files but can't change them.
questions.explanation: Managed settings are the enforcement layer: their deny rules can't be overridden by users or projects and block in every mode, including bypassPermissions (C). Personal settings (A) depend on each engineer and can be changed. CLAUDE.md (B) is guidance, not enforcement. Plan mode (D) still reads files, which is exactly the exposure security wants to prevent.

questions.stem: A risk lead is matching risks in an HR assistant to their primary mitigation. Match each risk to the control that addresses it most directly.
choices: Run tool queries under the requesting user's own permissions
Redact personal data before logs are written, with a retention limit
Require human approval for the action, enforced in code
Treat retrieved documents as untrusted data and limit what tools can do
rows: A manager asks the assistant for a colleague's salary and receives it because the assistant's service account can read all HR records.
A policy document edited by an employee contains hidden text telling the assistant to email the org chart outside the company.
The assistant can submit termination paperwork, and an error would harm an employee.
questions.explanation: Row 1: data exposure through a broad service account is fixed by querying with the requester's own permissions (A). Row 2: instructions hidden in a document are an injection risk, handled by treating content as data and restricting what tools can do (D). Row 3: a high-impact, hard-to-reverse action needs human approval enforced in code (C). Log redaction (B) protects personal data in logs, which isn't the risk in any of these three.

questions.stem: A company is drafting an acceptable-use policy for employees using Claude through its enterprise account. For each policy statement, select Yes if it is a sound policy statement.
statements: Employees may use the enterprise account for client work; personal AI accounts must not be used for confidential data.
Employees remain responsible for checking AI-assisted work before it is sent to clients or used in decisions.
Because the enterprise account has strong data terms, employees can paste any data into it without considering classification rules.
questions.explanation: Statement 1: Yes. Pointing confidential work to the approved tool, and away from personal accounts, is the core of a usable policy. Statement 2: Yes. Human accountability for AI-assisted work is a standard and necessary rule. Statement 3: No. Good vendor terms don't replace data classification rules; some data may still be restricted.

questions.stem: A governance team is assigning oversight levels to three Claude use cases at an insurer. Match each use case to the most appropriate level of human oversight.
choices: Fully automated, with sampled quality review
Human review of every output before it takes effect
Not suitable for automation with current controls
Automated with automatic escalation of flagged cases
rows: Suggesting tags for internal knowledge-base articles, which editors can change at any time.
Drafting letters that deny claims, which are sent to customers and can be appealed to a regulator.
Answering policyholders' routine coverage questions, where a classifier flags complaints and legal threats.
questions.explanation: Row 1: low-impact, easily corrected internal tags can run automatically with sampled review (A). Row 2: claim denials affect customers and regulators, so every letter needs human review before it is sent (B). Row 3: routine answers can be automated, with flagged complaints and legal threats escalated to people (D). None of these is so risky that automation is ruled out entirely (C).

questions.stem: In a kickoff meeting, a client's VP says the contract must guarantee '100% accurate answers' from the Claude-based policy assistant. How should you respond?
options: Agree to the requirement in principle, and define 'accurate' narrowly in the statement of work so it can be met with prompt tuning.
Explain that no AI or human process is 100% accurate, and propose a measured target on an agreed eval set, plus safeguards and monitoring.
Counter-propose 99.9% accuracy, which is achievable with a strong model and shows commitment to quality.
Decline the requirement and the engagement, since accepting a 100% guarantee would create contractual liability the firm can't carry.
questions.explanation: Setting realistic expectations early prevents later disputes. A measured target on an agreed test set, plus layered safeguards, is honest and verifiable. Agreeing to 100% (A) or picking an arbitrary near-perfect figure (C) creates commitments you cannot meet or prove. Refusing (D) abandons a solvable expectation problem.

questions.stem: You are running structured discovery for a proposed contract-review assistant. Which TWO pieces of information most change the architecture and should be gathered before any design work?
options: Who acts on the output and how: the reviewer workflow, approvals, latency expectations and integration points.
The full list of contract types the client might want to support in the next three years.
The current baseline (time, error rate, cost per contract) and the success metric the sponsor will judge by.
The client's preferred model vendor and version, so the design can be optimized for it from the start.
The visual style and branding guidelines the assistant's interface must follow.
questions.explanation: Baselines and success metrics define value (C), and the consuming workflow shapes the output format, latency targets and human review (A). Branding (E) matters for the interface but doesn't change the architecture. A vendor preference (D) is a late, secondary input that must pass your own constraints and evaluations. A three-year wish list (B) is scope for later phases, not what shapes the first architecture. Data sensitivity and residency constraints also belong in discovery.

questions.stem: A client insists on a 5-agent architecture for an HR FAQ assistant because 'multi-agent is the modern approach.' Your analysis suggests a single model with retrieval and two tools would suffice. What is the best way to handle this?
options: Build the 5-agent architecture as specified, since the client owns the requirements and has experience with the approach.
Build the single-model design and present it as a streamlined multi-agent system, since the client cares about the outcome.
Escalate to the client's executive sponsor to override the technical team's preference.
Ask what each agent uniquely needs, compare costs with a simpler design, and add agents only on evidence.
questions.explanation: Architects defend designs by naming costs and credible alternatives, and they ground decisions in what each component must uniquely do. Evidence-gated incrementalism respects the client's goal while avoiding unjustified complexity. Silent substitution (B) breaks trust. Escalation (C) is premature. Building five agents as specified (A) ignores the architect's job of naming costs and simpler alternatives.

questions.stem: You need approval for a design that uses prompt caching and a tiered-model router. Your audience is the CFO, who is not technical. Which explanation is most effective?
options: Translate it into business terms: projected cost per resolution, quality checks and the main risk.
Show a detailed table of token counts and prices per call for both designs, so the CFO can verify the arithmetic.
Walk through how caching stores computed state for the prompt prefix and how routing uses a classifier, so the CFO understands why it works.
Note that both techniques are documented best practices from the vendor, so they are low-risk by definition.
questions.explanation: Communicating trade-offs means translating them into the audience's terms: cost, risk and outcomes, with the evidence and the monitoring plan. Mechanism detail (B, C) fits engineers, not a CFO. An appeal to authority (D) gives no basis for a decision.

questions.stem: Six months after launch, a new engineering lead asks why the system uses full-context inclusion instead of RAG, and whether to switch. Nobody remembers the reasoning. Which practice would have prevented this?
options: Architecture decision records, including alternatives and triggers for revisiting.
A system overview page listing each component and technology in the architecture, kept in the wiki.
Recordings of all design meetings stored in the team's shared drive.
Detailed code comments in the retrieval and prompt-assembly modules explaining what the code does.
questions.explanation: ADRs preserve the why, including alternatives and the triggers for revisiting, which is exactly what a successor needs. Comments (D) describe code, not architecture. Meeting recordings (C) are unsearchable in practice. A technology list (B) omits the reasoning.

questions.stem: Your team is handing a production Claude application over to the client's operations team. Which TWO handoff artifacts are most important for them to run and evolve the system safely?
options: Runbooks and dashboards: what to monitor, alert thresholds, and incident and escalation procedures.
A list of prompt ideas the team tried and discarded during development.
The evaluation suite and how to run it before any change.
The full project plan and status reports, so the operations team understands how the system was built.
Recordings of the user-training sessions run during launch.
questions.explanation: Operating and changing an LLM system safely requires the means to test changes before they ship (C) and the means to detect and respond to problems (A). Discarded prompt ideas (B) are history, not operating material; what the client needs is the current, versioned prompts and configuration. Project plans (D) and training recordings (E) do not help the client operate or change the system.

questions.stem: A client wants a contractual SLA of 'responses in under 1 second.' Measurements show a median of 0.8 s and a p95 of 2.7 s for full answers, with time to first token at a p95 of 0.6 s when streaming. What SLA should you propose?
options: Accept the 1-second SLA measured as average full-response time, since the median is already 0.8 seconds.
Propose SLAs on p95 time to first token and p95 completion time, with a defined measurement method and exclusions.
Commit to a p99 of 1 second and plan an optimization sprint to reach it after launch.
Decline to commit to latency SLAs, since LLM response times depend on output length and so can't be promised in a contract.
questions.explanation: Align SLA expectations with how the system actually behaves and how users perceive it. Percentile-based and first-token metrics, with defined measurement, are realistic and verifiable. Averages (A) hide the tail. Refusing an SLA (D) is unhelpful. Committing to a target the data shows you will miss (C) is setting up a breach.

questions.stem: A large insurer wants Claude in 14 business processes at once. Budget and stakeholder patience are limited. What lifecycle approach do you recommend?
options: Let each business unit choose its own use case and vendor, so ownership stays with the people closest to the work.
Build a general-purpose AI platform for a year first, so all 14 processes can launch on a solid, consistent foundation.
Start with one or two high-volume, low-risk processes, prove results, then expand.
Launch all 14 in parallel with a shared platform team, so momentum builds and lessons are learned quickly across processes.
questions.explanation: A focused pilot with clear metrics produces evidence and reusable foundations, building stakeholder confidence for later phases. A big-bang launch (D) spreads effort and multiplies risk. A platform-first approach with no use cases (B) delays value. Fragmented vendors (A) lose shared governance.

questions.stem: Halfway through design, the client's legal team says, 'No customer data may leave our cloud account,' which rules out your planned use of the direct Claude API, its server-side web search and the Batches API. What is the best next step?
options: Present legal with industry examples of companies using the direct API, to show that the constraint is stricter than necessary.
Continue with the current design so the timeline holds, and work through the legal concern during the later security review.
Treat the constraint as a filter: redesign within it, quantify the impact on features, cost and timeline, and get sign-off.
Remove the affected features from the design and note the change in the next status report.
questions.explanation: Governance constraints rule options out before other trade-offs apply. The architect's job is to redesign within the constraint and communicate the consequences transparently. Deferring (B) creates rework and risk. Arguing (A) without a business case is unproductive. Silent scope changes (D) damage trust.

questions.stem: Business users of a newly launched sales-proposal assistant send scattered complaints through email and chat, and the engineering team cannot tell which issues matter most. What feedback-loop structure do you recommend?
options: Ask users to collect feedback until the next release, then review all of it together in a single prioritization session.
Contextual in-product feedback, regular triage with owners, and fixes tracked into evals.
Send a detailed satisfaction survey each quarter covering all features of the assistant.
Have the engineering team prioritize the backlog based on the technical severity of each reported issue.
questions.explanation: Effective lifecycle feedback is captured in context so it can be reproduced, triaged with business owners so it is prioritized by value, and closed into evaluations so fixes don't regress (B). Waiting until the next release (A) delays learning and loses context. A quarterly survey (C) is too coarse and too slow to locate specific failures. Prioritizing by technical severity alone (D) leaves out the business owners who understand the impact.

questions.stem: You must move a production assistant to a newer model version because the current one is scheduled for retirement. The new model's outputs are slightly more concise, and some users rely on the current format. What lifecycle steps are most appropriate?
options: Switch models on the retirement date, since both versions are from the same vendor and the API is unchanged.
Ask the vendor for an extended support agreement on the current model to avoid the migration.
Keep calling the current model ID after the retirement date, since retired models remain available at reduced capacity.
Run evals, adapt prompts, notify stakeholders and roll out in stages before the retirement date.
questions.explanation: Model lifecycle management means planned migrations: evaluate, adapt, communicate, roll out in stages and finish before the deadline. Surprise switches (A) break workflows. Indefinite extensions (B) cannot be assumed. Retired models will not keep serving requests (C).

questions.stem: A contact-center director announces to the board that the new AI assistant 'will replace 80% of agents within six months.' Your pilot shows 35% of contacts fully resolved without a human, with CSAT flat. What should you do?
options: Brief the director privately with the pilot data, and propose measured targets (deflection by contact type, handle time, CSAT) for the board.
Increase automatic resolution by closing more contacts without human handoff, moving closer to the stated goal.
Present the pilot data at the next board meeting to correct the record before expectations harden.
Leave it to the director, since board communication is the business owner's responsibility, and focus on improving the system.
questions.explanation: Expectation alignment is part of the architect's role. Correcting an unsupported claim privately, with data and a constructive alternative, protects the project and the stakeholder relationship. Silence (D) lets a failure narrative form. Public contradiction (C) damages trust. Gaming the metric (B) harms customers.

questions.stem: A sponsor's only requirement for the next iteration is 'make the assistant smarter.' How should you turn this into actionable requirements?
options: Turn 'smarter' into measurable targets based on the failures that matter to the sponsor.
Expand the system prompt with more detailed instructions and examples covering common question types.
Increase the context window and retrieve more documents per question, so the assistant has more information to work with.
Upgrade to the most capable model available and report the benchmark improvement to the sponsor.
questions.explanation: Vague goals must become specific, measurable requirements grounded in observed failures; otherwise no change can be shown to succeed. Jumping to a bigger model (D), more instructions (B) or more context (C) may not address the actual problem, and their success cannot be measured against 'smarter.'

questions.stem: An executive asks: 'Our product catalog changes weekly. Should we fine-tune Claude on it so it knows our products?' What is the best explanation?
options: No change is needed, since large models are trained on public web data that includes most product catalogs.
Supply changing facts at request time via retrieval or tools; fine-tuning suits behavior, not facts.
Yes: fine-tune on the catalog weekly, which builds product knowledge into the model and avoids retrieval latency.
Fine-tune once on the full catalog and use the system prompt to list the weekly changes.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is knowledge versus behavior. Changing facts should flow in at request time, where they are current, traceable and correctable. Weekly retraining (C) is costly and always lags. Claude does not know a private catalog (A). A one-time fine-tune (D) becomes stale.

questions.stem: Three months after launch, quality has slowly degraded and nobody noticed until a customer escalation. The project team had disbanded after go-live. What lifecycle gap does this reveal?
options: No defined post-launch owner or cadence for monitoring, eval maintenance and content updates.
The model was too small for the workload, and its limitations became visible as usage grew.
Users' question patterns shifted, which no design can anticipate in advance.
The user interface encouraged vague questions, which gradually lowered answer quality.
questions.explanation: AI systems need ongoing operation: monitoring, refreshed evaluations, content upkeep and periodic reviews, with clear owners. Lifecycle planning must extend past go-live (A). A model that was too small (B) would have shown problems at launch, not a slow decline. Shifting question patterns (C) are expected, and monitoring with an owner is how you catch them. The interface (D) didn't change. Each of these looks for a technical cause of an ownership gap.

questions.stem: You must present an architecture recommendation to a steering committee that includes legal, finance and engineering leaders. Which document structure is most effective?
options: A concise decision document with alternatives, costs, risks and the decisions needed.
A complete technical specification covering every component, shared the night before so the committee can review it in depth.
A high-level diagram of the chosen technologies and vendors, with a short narrative of the expected benefits.
A live demonstration of the prototype, followed by open discussion of any questions.
questions.explanation: Mixed audiences need the decision framed with alternatives, costs, risks and an explicit request, with depth available but not leading. A dense spec (B) will not be read. A technology diagram with benefits only (C) says nothing about trade-offs. A demo (D) shows capability, not the decision rationale or risk position.

questions.stem: Mid-project, the client asks that the read-only support assistant also be allowed to issue credits and modify subscriptions 'since it's already integrated.' What is the right response?
options: Decline, since support assistants should remain read-only to avoid any risk of financial errors.
Add the write tools now, since the integration and authentication already exist and the request is a small extension.
Treat it as a formal scope change: reassess the risks, update governance sign-off, then agree.
Add the tools behind a feature flag and enable them after launch once usage stabilizes.
questions.explanation: Moving from read to write changes the risk profile completely. It requires a fresh risk assessment, new controls and stakeholder approval, handled as a formal scope change. Casual addition (B, D) bypasses governance. Blanket refusal (A) ignores that write actions can be done safely with the right controls.

questions.stem: A client asks how they will know, two weeks after launch, whether a claims-intake assistant is on track to deliver value. Which TWO metrics are the best early indicators to agree on up front?
options: Total tokens consumed per week, which shows how much work the assistant is doing.
Quality and risk indicators: audited extraction accuracy on a weekly sample, escalation and not-found rates, and incidents.
Rework rate and adjuster time per claim compared with the baseline.
Adoption indicators such as weekly active users and sessions per user, which show whether staff are using it.
The number of features shipped since launch, which shows the team's delivery velocity.
questions.explanation: Early indicators should connect to the eventual business outcome (rework, time saved against the baseline) and guard against quality and risk failures. Adoption (D) shows usage, not value. Token volume (A) and features shipped (E) measure activity, not value.

questions.stem: During discovery, a business owner describes the desired assistant in detail, but frontline staff who will use it describe a different workflow and different pain points. What should you do?
options: Observe the actual workflow, then reconcile both groups' views around measurable outcomes and record open conflicts.
Follow the business owner's description, since they sponsor the project and are accountable for its outcomes.
Follow the frontline staff's description, since they will use the system daily and know the real workflow.
Design two variants of the assistant, one for each group's workflow, and let usage decide.
questions.explanation: Requirements gathering must surface and resolve conflicting perspectives using evidence. Siding with one group (B, C) risks building the wrong thing or losing sponsorship. Two assistants (D) doubles cost without resolving the disagreement.

questions.stem: After a model upgrade, users report that the assistant's tone became more formal. Accuracy improved on all evaluations. Some stakeholders want to roll back. How should you handle it?
options: Keep the new model and treat the complaints as an adjustment period, since every evaluation improved.
Add a formality setting so each user can choose the tone they prefer.
Weigh both measurably, try a targeted tone fix, and decide on agreed criteria.
Roll back to the previous model, since user satisfaction is the primary measure of success.
questions.explanation: Lifecycle decisions should weigh measured trade-offs against agreed criteria, and often a targeted fix keeps the gains while addressing the concern. Rolling back reflexively (D) loses real improvements. Ignoring users (A) erodes adoption. Unevaluated settings (B) add untested variants.

questions.stem: An eval of a claims assistant shows 92% of answers are correct. The remaining 8% include a few answers that told customers they were covered when they weren't. How should you report this to the executive sponsor?
options: Report the 92% headline, since one clear number is easiest for executives to act on.
Report the 92%, then break the 8% down by severity, with real examples of the serious errors.
Hold the report until the accuracy is above 95%, so the sponsor isn't worried by a low number.
Report the per-category F1 scores for all claim types, with the full statistical method attached.
questions.explanation: Executives need to know both how often it's right and how bad the misses are. Telling someone they're covered when they're not is a far bigger risk than a typo, so show the severity and concrete examples (B). A single number hides the serious errors (A). Withholding results damages trust and delays the decision (C). A full metrics table without context is hard for a sponsor to act on (D).

questions.stem: A claims assistant is ready to launch to 2,000 adjusters. Which TWO steps make the rollout safest?
options: Run it in shadow mode first, producing drafts that adjusters can compare but don't send.
Roll out in stages, such as 5% of adjusters, then 25%, then everyone, with checks at each step.
Launch to all 2,000 adjusters on the same day, so that everyone gets the same training.
Wait until the eval shows 100% accuracy, so no issues can appear after launch.
Launch quietly without telling adjusters, so their reactions don't affect the results.
questions.explanation: Shadow mode tests the system on real work with no customer impact (A). A staged rollout limits how many people a problem can reach and gives checkpoints to stop or roll back (B). A big-bang launch exposes everyone at once (C). 100% accuracy is not a realistic bar (D). Users need to know they're working with AI output to review it properly (E).

questions.stem: A team is about to launch a new prompt version. The sponsor asks, 'If it goes badly, how will we know to roll back?' What is the best answer?
options: We'll watch user feedback closely for the first few weeks and decide together whether the results feel worse than before.
We agreed thresholds before launch, such as an escalation rate above 12%, and crossing one triggers a rollback.
We'll roll back if any single user complains, since one complaint can point to a wider problem.
We won't need to roll back, because the new prompt scored higher on the offline eval set.
questions.explanation: Rollback criteria should be specific, measurable and agreed before launch, so the decision is quick and not a debate (B). 'Feels worse' is too vague to act on quickly (A). A single complaint is noise, not a reliable trigger (C). Offline evals don't catch everything real traffic exposes (D).

questions.stem: Anthropic announces that the model version used by three of your client's applications will be retired in six months. What is the best plan?
options: Wait until the last month, since a newer model is usually better and needs no testing.
Switch all three applications to an alias that points to the newest model, so future retirements need no action.
List every place the model ID is used, run each app's eval on the replacement, then migrate in stages.
Ask Anthropic to keep the old model running longer for this client, so no change is needed.
questions.explanation: A planned migration means finding every use of the model, testing the replacement against each app's eval set, fixing any differences, and moving over in stages well before the deadline (C). Newer models can behave differently, such as different tone, format or tool use, so waiting risks a rushed change (A). An alias makes future changes happen silently (B). Retirement dates generally don't move, so this isn't a plan (D).

questions.stem: Finance asks how much the support assistant costs. The engineering dashboard shows 1.2 billion tokens last month. What is the most useful way to report cost?
options: Report total tokens by model, since tokens are what the provider actually bills.
Report cost per resolved ticket and per user, compared with the cost of the old process.
Report the provider's price per million tokens, so finance can do the math themselves for any period.
Report the month-over-month change in token count, since growth is what finance cares about.
questions.explanation: Finance needs cost in business units they can compare: cost per resolved ticket or per user, set against what the old process cost (B). Raw tokens (A), a price list (C) or token growth (D) don't tell them whether the system is worth its cost.

questions.stem: An engineer edited a production system prompt directly to fix one customer's complaint. The change broke answer formatting for thousands of other users. What process change prevents this?
options: Only senior engineers may edit the production prompt, after asking the team lead in chat.
Prompts live in version control; every change runs the eval suite and goes out through a staged release.
Freeze the prompt after the launch date, so that no further changes of any kind can be made to it.
Keep a backup copy of the prompt in a shared document, so it can be pasted back if needed.
questions.explanation: Prompts are code, and treating them like code means review, automated eval checks and staged rollout, which catches regressions before they reach everyone (B). Seniority doesn't catch regressions (A). A freeze stops necessary fixes (C). A backup helps you recover but doesn't prevent the break (D).

questions.stem: A client wants to start a 6-week pilot of a document-summarization assistant for underwriters. What should be agreed before the pilot starts?
options: The list of features to add after the pilot, so the team can start building them right away.
How success will be measured, including today's baseline, such as current minutes per file.
The final production budget, so the pilot can be sized to fit within it.
Which model will be used, since changing models partway through a pilot invalidates the results.
questions.explanation: Without agreed success measures and a baseline, a pilot ends in opinions, not evidence. Measuring today's minutes per file, error rate and so on before starting makes the result clear (B). The feature list (A) and production budget (C) depend on what the pilot shows. The model choice matters less than having a way to judge the result (D).

questions.stem: A sponsor's business case says the assistant will save 20 minutes per case across 10,000 cases a year. The pilot shows each AI draft still needs 6 minutes of human review. How should the business case be updated?
options: Keep the 20 minutes, since review time is part of normal work and shouldn't be counted.
Count the net saving, 20 minus 6 minutes, and include review time and usage costs in the case.
Double the case volume estimate to make up for the review time, so the total savings stay the same.
Drop the business case, since any review time means the assistant doesn't save effort.
questions.explanation: An honest business case uses the net saving per case, which here is 14 minutes, and includes the cost of human review and model usage (B). Ignoring review time overstates the benefit (A). Inflating volume to hit a target is misleading (C). A 14-minute saving per case can still be a strong case (D).

questions.stem: Two weeks before launch, testing shows the assistant can't handle scanned handwritten forms, which make up 15% of the client's documents. What should you do?
options: Launch as planned, and fix handwriting support in a later release without raising it with the sponsor before launch.
Tell the sponsor now, with the impact and two or three options, such as routing those forms to people.
Delay the launch quietly by reporting other, smaller issues until handwriting support is ready.
Remove handwritten forms from the test set, so the results match the launch criteria.
questions.explanation: Surface the problem early, with what it affects and concrete options, so the sponsor can decide (B). For example, launch for typed forms and send handwritten ones to people. Hiding it (A, C) destroys trust when it comes out. Changing the test set to pass hides a real gap (D).

questions.stem: A month after launch, only 20% of the sales team uses the proposal assistant. Interviews show reps don't trust its pricing tables and find it slower than their old templates. What is the best next step?
options: Make use of the assistant mandatory, and track each rep's usage in the weekly sales meeting for a quarter.
Fix the pricing table issue, show reps the evidence, and work with a few reps on the slow steps.
Switch to a more capable model, since a smarter model will win the reps over on its own.
Run a company-wide training session on prompt writing, so that reps can get better results from the tool.
questions.explanation: Low adoption has specific causes here: trust in the numbers and speed. Fix those and show the reps it's fixed, working with them directly (B). Forcing use without fixing the problems breeds workarounds (A). A different model may not fix pricing errors that come from data or retrieval (C). Prompt training doesn't address either complaint (D).

questions.stem: A compliance manager tests the assistant twice with the same question, worded slightly differently, and gets two answers that are both correct but phrased differently. She worries it's 'unreliable.' What is the best response?
options: Promise that answers will be word-for-word identical after a configuration change is made.
Explain that wording varies but the facts shouldn't, and show the eval that checks facts across rephrasings.
Tell her that this behavior is normal for AI systems and no further action is needed.
Suggest she asks questions with the same wording each time, so that the answers she gets stay word-for-word consistent.
questions.explanation: Address the real concern, which is whether the facts are reliable, with evidence: an eval that asks the same question in different ways and checks the facts match (B). Identical wording can't be guaranteed (A). Dismissing the concern without evidence doesn't build trust (C). Users can't be expected to always phrase things the same way (D).

questions.stem: A client's legal team asks what could go wrong with a contract-summary assistant before they approve it. Which TWO points should your answer cover?
options: It can occasionally state a clause that isn't in the contract, so summaries cite the clause they come from.
Lawyers review every summary before it's used in a decision, and you'll measure how often they correct it.
Errors are unlikely to matter because the model reads the whole contract instead of relying on memory.
The model has been trained on legal documents, so its summaries are as reliable as a lawyer's.
Any errors will be the vendor's responsibility, so the legal team doesn't need to plan for them.
questions.explanation: Be specific about the failure mode, invented or misstated clauses, and the mitigation of citations back to the source (A), and about the human check and how you'll track it (B). Errors are still possible even when the full text is in context (C). Training on legal text doesn't make it as reliable as a lawyer (D). Contracts rarely shift that responsibility, and the client still needs a plan (E).

questions.stem: You're starting an AI project in a large company. The sponsor and the IT team are on board. Three months in, the security team and the works council block the launch over issues no one raised earlier. What should have been done at the start?
options: Keep the project quiet until it was finished, so that no group could slow it down.
Map every group that can approve or block it, such as security, legal, privacy and staff representatives, and involve them early.
Ask the sponsor to overrule any group that raises concerns late in the project.
Build the project outside the company network to avoid security reviews.
questions.explanation: A stakeholder map at kickoff names everyone with approval or veto power, so their requirements shape the design instead of blocking the launch (B). Secrecy makes the late block worse (A). Overruling security or staff representatives is rarely possible or wise (C). Working around security creates real risk (D).

questions.stem: A sponsor wants the assistant to be 'faster, cheaper and more accurate' all at once. Your tests show the most accurate setup is also the slowest and most expensive. How should you present this?
options: Promise all three improvements, then decide later which one to quietly give up.
Show two or three concrete options with their measured accuracy, cost and speed, and ask which matters most.
Pick the option you think is best yourself, and present it to the sponsor as the only setup that's technically possible.
Tell the sponsor that the trade-off is too technical to explain in detail.
questions.explanation: Make the trade-off concrete: a few real options, each with measured numbers, let the sponsor decide based on business priorities (B). Overpromising damages trust (A). Hiding options takes the decision away from the person who owns it (C). The trade-off can be explained in plain terms (D).

questions.stem: A demo of a contract assistant impressed executives using five hand-picked contracts. They now expect launch next week. What should you do?
options: Launch next week, since the demo proved that the system works.
Explain that the demo wasn't representative, and share eval results on real contracts plus the steps to launch.
Run the same demo again for a wider audience, so that more people see it working.
Delay the launch indefinitely without explaining why.
questions.explanation: Demos show what's possible on chosen examples. Set expectations with results on a realistic sample, including failures, and a clear plan to production (B). Launching on demo evidence risks a public failure (A). More demos reinforce the wrong impression (C). An unexplained delay damages trust (D).

questions.stem: Users of a claims assistant correct its drafts every day. The corrections are saved, but no one looks at them. What process turns this into improvement?
options: Delete the corrections each month to save storage space.
Review the corrections regularly, add representative ones to the eval set, and use them to target fixes.
Fine-tune a new model every night on all of the corrections.
Show all of the saved corrections to the model in every future request, so that it learns from them automatically over time.
questions.explanation: User corrections show real failures. Reviewing them, adding good examples to the eval set and fixing the causes closes the feedback loop (B). Deleting them wastes the signal (A). Nightly fine-tuning is costly and unreviewed (C). Adding every correction to each request would bloat the context and wouldn't scale (D).

questions.stem: An assistant launched four months ago. The project team moved on, and the business owner only hears about problems when customers complain. What ongoing practice should be set up?
options: A yearly review of the system, held at the start of each budget cycle.
A regular review with the business owner covering quality metrics, cost, incidents and planned changes.
A rule that issues are discussed only when a customer formally complains.
A dashboard that tracks only the total number of conversations each day.
questions.explanation: A regular operating review, monthly for example, with clear owners, quality and cost trends, incidents and upcoming changes such as model updates, keeps the system healthy (B). A yearly review is too slow (A). Waiting for complaints means reacting too late (C). Volume alone says nothing about quality (D).

questions.stem: Next week's update will change how the assistant formats answers and add a new data source. How should users be told?
options: Don't tell users, since they will notice the changes on their own.
Send short release notes before the change saying what's different, why, and where to report problems.
Send all users a detailed technical document describing the new model settings, prompt changes and the new data source's schema.
Tell users only if they complain about the new behavior.
questions.explanation: Short, plain release notes ahead of time explain what will change and where to send feedback, which reduces confusion and support tickets (B). Silent changes surprise users (A). Technical detail isn't useful to most users (C). Waiting for complaints damages trust (D).

questions.stem: An executive wants to skip evaluation entirely to hit a launch date in two weeks. What is the best response?
options: Agree, and plan to build evaluations after launch if any problems come up.
Propose a small eval on the highest-risk cases plus a limited launch with clear rollback criteria.
Refuse to launch until a full eval suite of several thousand cases has been built, run and reviewed, however long that takes.
Escalate to the CEO immediately, without offering any alternative plan.
questions.explanation: Offer a path that meets the date while managing risk: a focused eval on the riskiest cases and a limited first rollout with agreed rollback triggers (B). Skipping evaluation entirely risks a public failure (A). Insisting on everything ignores a real business constraint (C). Escalating without options isn't constructive (D).

questions.stem: Loan officers start using an assistant that summarizes applications. What training matters most for them?
options: How large language models work internally, including attention, transformers and how they are trained on text.
What it does well, where it's known to make mistakes, and how to check its summaries quickly.
How to write prompts from scratch for every possible type of question.
How to turn the assistant off whenever it gives a wrong answer.
questions.explanation: Users need practical knowledge: strengths, known failure patterns and a quick way to verify outputs, so they rely on it appropriately (B). Model internals don't help daily use (A). Prompt-writing skill matters less when the app already handles the prompt (C). Turning it off doesn't teach them to use it well (D).

questions.stem: A requirement says 'The assistant should give accurate answers about benefits.' How should it be rewritten so the team can test it?
options: 'The assistant should give highly accurate answers about all benefits topics.'
'On the 300-question benefits eval set, at least 95% of answers are correct and none give wrong eligibility facts.'
'The assistant should give answers that users are happy with most of the time.'
'The assistant should be as accurate as the best human benefits expert.'
questions.explanation: Testable acceptance criteria name the test set, the measure and the threshold, including zero tolerance for the most harmful error (B). 'Highly accurate' (A) and 'happy most of the time' (C) can't be checked. 'As accurate as the best expert' has no defined test (D).

questions.stem: Procurement asks why the team chose Claude through Amazon Bedrock instead of the direct Claude API. Which explanation is most useful?
options: 'Bedrock gets new Claude features first, so it is the more capable option for an enterprise like ours.'
'We already have AWS contracts, billing and data controls, so Bedrock fits; we checked the features we need are available there.'
'The direct API is less secure than Bedrock, so it can't be used by large companies.'
'The choice doesn't matter, since both platforms are identical in every way.'
questions.explanation: Explain the decision in procurement's terms: existing contracts, billing, compliance and data controls, plus a check that the needed features are available, since new features can reach the direct API first (B). (A) is often the reverse. The direct API isn't insecure (C). The platforms differ in some features and operations (D).

questions.stem: A company is retiring an internal assistant that a new system will replace. What does a responsible shutdown include?
options: Turning it off on a Friday evening without notice, so that users are pushed to switch to the new system over the weekend.
Telling users the date and the alternative in advance, moving needed data or workflows, and deleting data per policy.
Leaving it running indefinitely next to the new system, so that users can choose.
Deleting all of its data immediately, including records the company must keep.
questions.explanation: Retirement needs notice, a clear alternative, migration of needed workflows or data, and handling of stored data under the retention policy (B). A surprise shutdown disrupts work (A). Running both indefinitely doubles cost and confusion (C). Deleting records that must be kept can break legal requirements (D).

questions.stem: Halfway through the quarter, the assistant's model spending is 40% over budget because usage grew faster than expected. How should you report it?
options: Wait until the end of the quarter, in case usage happens to fall again.
Report it now with the cause and options, such as caching, a smaller model for simple requests, or shorter outputs, with savings for each.
Cut the service off for some users without telling them, to stay within the budget.
Report only the total overspend, and let finance decide what to cut.
questions.explanation: Raise budget problems early, explain what's driving them, and bring costed options so the business can choose (B). Waiting makes it worse (A). Quietly cutting users off is a business decision taken without the business (C). A number without options leaves finance guessing (D).

questions.stem: A customer escalates after the assistant told them a fee would be waived, which contradicts the official policy. The service director asks for an explanation. What is the best response?
options: Say that AI systems sometimes make mistakes like this, that it was a one-off, and that nothing can really be done to prevent it.
Explain the cause found in the logs, the immediate fix, how you'll prevent it, and how the customer is being handled.
Blame the customer for wording their question in a confusing way.
Promise that the assistant won't make this kind of mistake again, and offer the customer a goodwill credit.
questions.explanation: A good incident explanation covers what happened (from the logs, such as an outdated policy chunk being retrieved), what was done right away, what prevents a repeat (fixing the index and adding the case to evals), and how the customer is being taken care of (B). Saying nothing can be done (A), blaming the user (C) or promising perfection (D) don't build trust.

questions.stem: A steering committee asks for a one-page update on a claims-summarization pilot. Results: handling time fell from 22 to 14 minutes per claim, summary accuracy against adjuster review is 94%, two summaries omitted a policy exclusion, and monthly run cost is $11,000 against $46,000 of saved adjuster time. Which framing is most useful to the committee?
options: Lead with the model and architecture choices, then token usage by month, then the accuracy figure, since the committee needs the technical details to approve the next phase.
Lead with time and cost saved, state the 94% accuracy and the two exclusion misses with the fix in place, and end with the decision needed and its risks.
Report only the time and cost savings, since mentioning the two misses would undermine confidence in a pilot that is clearly succeeding.
Send the full evaluation spreadsheet with all 1,200 scored summaries, so committee members can draw their own conclusions from the raw data.
questions.explanation: Executives need business outcomes first, an honest account of risks with what has been done about them, and a clear decision request (B). Leading with architecture and tokens (A) buries the value. Hiding the misses (C) damages trust when they surface, and omissions of exclusions are exactly what the committee must weigh. Raw data (D) pushes analysis onto the audience.

questions.stem: A client's head of customer service asks you to set expectations for a new Claude-based email assistant before launch. For each statement you might make, select Yes if it is accurate and appropriate.
statements: 'It will sometimes be wrong, so agents review drafts for refund and legal topics, and we will report the correction rate every week.'
'Because it reads your policies, it can't give an answer that contradicts them.'
'Quality is measured on an agreed set of real emails, and we will re-check it whenever prompts, policies or the model change.'
questions.explanation: Statement 1: Yes. It is honest about errors and explains the safeguard and how it will be measured. Statement 2: No. Grounding reduces but doesn't remove contradictions, so promising otherwise sets false expectations. Statement 3: Yes. It ties quality to an agreed measurement and to re-testing on change.

questions.stem: Six months after go-live, a client's operations team owns a Claude-based underwriting assistant. Anthropic announces the retirement of the model version it uses, effective in five months. The client's IT director asks who should do what. What is the best lifecycle response?
options: Tell the client that the vendor's retirement notice is the vendor's responsibility, so no action is needed until the retirement date.
Offer to handle the migration for the client, since only the original delivery team understands the system well enough to change the model.
Advise switching to an alias that points at the latest model, so future retirements happen automatically without anyone needing to plan or test them in advance.
Follow the runbook: the operations owner inventories where the model ID is used, runs the evals on the replacement and plans a staged rollout.
questions.explanation: Lifecycle planning should already assign an owner and a process for model retirements, run by the client's operations team using the handover eval suite (D). Waiting (A) risks an outage when the model stops serving. Making the delivery team indispensable (B) undermines the handover. A floating alias (C) changes behavior without evaluation.

questions.stem: A delivery lead is preparing messages about a Claude-based assistant for three audiences. Match each audience to the framing that serves it best.
choices: Business outcomes against the baseline, risks and the decision needed
Architecture, evaluation method and known failure modes
What the tool does, what it doesn't, and how to report problems
Token counts and model version history
rows: The executive sponsor deciding whether to fund a company-wide rollout.
The frontline staff who will use the assistant from next Monday.
The client's architecture review board, which must approve the design.
questions.explanation: Row 1: a funding decision needs outcomes against the baseline, risks and a clear ask (A). Row 2: users need to know what the tool does and doesn't do, and how to report problems (C). Row 3: a review board needs the design, how quality is measured and where it can fail (B). Token counts and version history (D) are operational details that none of these audiences needs as the main message.

questions.stem: A pilot of a Claude-based proposal assistant is ending. The client asks for a recommendation on whether to scale it. For each element of your recommendation, select Yes if it belongs in it.
statements: Results against the success metrics agreed at the start of the pilot, including where targets were missed.
A statement that the assistant will perform better in production because users will get used to it.
The conditions for scaling, such as owners, monitoring, budget and an evaluation process for future changes.
questions.explanation: Statement 1: Yes. A recommendation should rest on the pre-agreed metrics, reported honestly, including misses. Statement 2: No. It is an unsupported prediction; any expected improvement needs evidence. Statement 3: Yes. Scaling safely needs owners, monitoring, budget and a change process, and the client needs to see them.

questions.stem: A client is moving a Claude-based assistant from pilot to long-term operation. Match each lifecycle activity to the role that should own it.
choices: The business owner of the process
The platform or operations team
The security and compliance team
The vendor's account team
rows: Deciding whether a drop in answer quality on billing questions is acceptable or must be fixed before the next release.
Watching latency, error rates and cost dashboards, and responding to alerts.
Reviewing whether a new data source can be connected under the company's data-handling rules.
questions.explanation: Row 1: whether a quality trade-off is acceptable is a business decision for the process owner (A). Row 2: day-to-day monitoring and alert response belong to the platform or operations team (B). Row 3: approving new data sources under data-handling rules is a security and compliance task (C). The vendor's account team (D) supports the client but doesn't own any of these decisions.

questions.stem: A team's CLAUDE.md says 'Always run the linter and formatter before finishing.' Code from Claude Code sessions still occasionally arrives in PRs with lint errors. What change gives a reliable guarantee in the developer workflow?
options: Add PostToolUse and Stop hooks that run the linter, with CI as the final merge gate.
Package the lint procedure as a Skill, so Claude loads detailed linting instructions whenever it edits code.
Require plan mode for every task, so each plan includes a linting step that the developer reviews and approves.
Strengthen the CLAUDE.md instruction with the exact lint commands, an example of a clean run, and a note that unlinted code will be rejected.
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is guidance; hooks run deterministically at defined points in Claude Code's lifecycle, and CI enforces the standard at merge regardless of who wrote the code. Emphasis (D), Skills (B) and plan mode (C) remain guidance-level and do not guarantee that lint runs.

questions.stem: In a monorepo, test files live next to the code they test throughout hundreds of folders (for example src/**/foo.test.ts). The team wants testing conventions applied only when Claude works on test files, without loading them for every task. What is the best configuration?
options: Add the testing conventions to the root CLAUDE.md under a 'Testing' heading, so Claude has them available in every session.
Create a 'tests' Skill containing the conventions, and ask developers to invoke it when writing tests.
Create a rule file in .claude/rules/ (for example testing.md) whose paths frontmatter lists globs such as '**/*.test.ts'.
Create a CLAUDE.md in a top-level tests/ folder containing the conventions, which Claude loads whenever it works on tests.
questions.explanation: Path-scoped rules match by glob, so they cover file types scattered across the repository and load only when relevant. Root CLAUDE.md (A) loads always. A folder CLAUDE.md (D) only covers that one folder. A manually invoked Skill (B) depends on people remembering to use it.

questions.stem: A CI job runs Claude Code to review every pull request and post findings as a comment. The job sometimes hangs, and on other runners it behaves differently because of developers' personal hooks and plugins on shared images. Which invocation pattern addresses both problems?
options: Run claude -p --bare with explicit settings, scoped --allowedTools, JSON output and exit codes.
Run claude in an interactive session inside tmux on the runner, with a script that sends the review prompt and captures the output.
Copy a reference developer's ~/.claude directory onto every runner, so all runners share the same hooks and plugins.
Run claude -p with --dangerously-skip-permissions, so the job doesn't stop to wait for an approval prompt.
questions.explanation: Print mode runs once and exits, so nothing waits for input. Bare mode gives the same result on every machine by not loading whatever happens to be configured locally. Explicit tool approval, JSON output and exit codes make the job scriptable and safe. Interactive sessions (B) can hang. Skipping all permissions (D) removes safety. Copying personal configuration (C) adds variability.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants one Claude Code policy (allowed MCP servers, deny rules for secrets) for most engineers, but a stricter policy for the payments team. They plan to use server-managed settings in the Claude.ai admin console for both. What limitation should you flag, and how do you work around it?
options: Managed settings can be overridden by project settings, so the payments team should commit a stricter .claude/settings.json in their repos.
The console can't target groups yet; deploy the stricter policy via MDM or a managed file.
No limitation: the admin console supports separate managed policies per group, assigned through the identity provider.
Ask the payments team to add the stricter rules to their user settings, with periodic checks by the security team.
questions.explanation: Claude Code's documentation notes that the console applies one policy to everyone it reaches and cannot target groups yet, while file and MDM delivery can target specific machines. Managed settings cannot be overridden by users (A). User settings (D) are not enforcement. The console does not support separate policies per group (C).

questions.stem: Thirty repositories each have copied versions of the same Claude Code skills, subagents and hooks, and they have drifted. What is the best way to share and update them centrally?
options: Assign one owner per repository to keep its copies in sync with a shared reference document.
Consolidate all skills, subagents and hooks into one comprehensive CLAUDE.md that every repository includes.
Package them as a plugin in a team marketplace and register that marketplace for everyone through managed settings.
A scheduled job that copies a reference .claude folder into all 30 repositories each night, opening a PR when anything changed.
questions.explanation: Plugins and marketplaces are the distribution mechanism for shared Claude Code capabilities: update once and every consumer gets the change, while repository-specific guidance stays local. Copy scripts (D) create churn and conflicts. A giant CLAUDE.md (B) loads everything every session. Per-team copies (A) are the current drift problem.

questions.stem: During a long debugging session in a large repository, Claude Code's responses degrade after it has read dozens of large log files and source files. What is the most effective way to continue?
options: Use subagents for exploration, compact or restart with a summary, and keep a notes file.
Re-paste the most important log excerpts so they are recent in the conversation and easier for Claude to focus on.
Switch to a model with a larger context window and continue in the same session with all files still loaded.
Continue in the same session but ask Claude to focus only on the most recent files it read.
questions.explanation: Context hygiene keeps sessions effective: subagents isolate exploratory reading, compaction or a fresh session with a handoff clears clutter, and persistent notes preserve what matters. Re-pasting logs (B) makes it worse. A bigger window (C) postpones the problem and still dilutes attention. Asking Claude to focus on recent files (D) doesn't remove the older files from its context.

questions.stem: A nightly job runs claude -p 'Update the dependency pins and run the tests'. Logs show that Bash commands for the package manager and the test runner were denied and the run finished without changes. No permission mode or allow rules were configured. Why, and what is the fix?
options: The model judged dependency updates to be risky and declined; rephrase the prompt to explain that the change is approved.
The run exceeded its output budget; raise max output tokens so the commands can complete.
Unattended runs deny any call that needs approval; pre-approve the exact commands needed with --allowedTools.
Print mode does not support Bash commands; run the task in an interactive session on a scheduled machine instead.
questions.explanation: With no one present, anything that would prompt is denied unless rules, hooks or a permission mode resolve it, so unattended runs must declare what is allowed. Bash is supported in print mode (D). The denial came from the permission system, not a model refusal (A). Token limits (B) are unrelated.

questions.stem: An engineer must refactor an unfamiliar authentication module that touches many files, and the security team wants to review the approach before any code changes. Which Claude Code workflow fits best?
options: Use print mode to generate a single patch file for security to review before applying.
Have Claude implement the refactor on a branch, then revert if security objects to the approach.
Plan mode: explore and draft a plan without edits, have it reviewed, then implement it.
Run with acceptEdits so changes are made quickly, then have security review the full diff before merging.
questions.explanation: Plan mode is designed for exploring unfamiliar code and reviewing the approach of large or sensitive changes before any edits. Reviewing only after edits (B, D) skips the requested pre-change review. A one-shot patch (A) gives no interactive planning or approval step.

questions.stem: A developer added personal permission tweaks and a local MCP server with a test token to .claude/settings.json and committed it, so teammates received both. How should Claude Code configuration be split?
options: Keep everything in .claude/settings.json and document which entries are personal, so teammates can remove what they don't need.
Move all configuration into CLAUDE.md, which is easier to read and review than JSON settings.
Keep the token in .claude/settings.json but make the repository private, so only team members can see it.
Commit shared settings in .claude/settings.json, keep personal overrides in .claude/settings.local.json, and reference secrets through environment variables.
questions.explanation: Claude Code's layering separates shared project configuration, personal project overrides and personal global settings, and secrets stay out of version control. Making the repository private (C) does not make committed secrets safe. CLAUDE.md (B) is for instructions, not settings. Documenting which entries are personal (A) still ships personal settings and the token to every teammate.

questions.stem: An on-call team wants Claude Code to help investigate production incidents by reading logs, metrics and recent deploy history. What is the safest effective setup?
options: Give Claude Code production admin credentials during incidents, so it can investigate and apply fixes without delay.
Export recent production database snapshots into the session, so Claude can analyze the data directly.
Provide read-only access through scoped tools or MCP servers for logs, metrics and deploy history, keeping remediation with humans or behind approval.
Turn off permission prompts for the on-call team's sessions, so investigations are not slowed down.
questions.explanation: Operational support benefits from fast, broad read access, while changes during incidents carry high risk. Read-only scoped access with human-controlled remediation and an audit trail gives speed without new failure modes. Admin credentials (A) and disabled prompts (D) remove safety under pressure. Database dumps (B) expose sensitive data unnecessarily.

questions.stem: A CI job runs Claude Code unattended. It must be allowed to run only a fixed list of approved commands, and anything else must be refused automatically instead of hanging while it waits for approval. Which permission mode fits?
options: default mode, so Claude stops and asks for approval whenever it needs to run a new command.
acceptEdits mode, so file edits are approved and other commands still prompt.
dontAsk mode with allow rules, so anything not pre-approved is denied automatically.
bypassPermissions mode, so no command ever stops to wait for an approval.
questions.explanation: dontAsk denies anything that would need a prompt and runs only what your allow rules cover, which is ideal for locked-down CI (C). default and acceptEdits still prompt, and with no one there to answer, the job hangs (A, B). bypassPermissions removes all checks, the opposite of 'only approved commands' (D).

questions.stem: A developer asks when it is acceptable to run Claude Code in bypassPermissions mode, which skips all permission checks. What is the correct guidance?
options: On developer laptops, for experienced engineers who carefully review every diff afterward.
Inside an isolated, disposable container that has no access to production systems or secrets.
In CI for any repository, as long as the pipeline only runs on a protected branch.
Whenever auto mode isn't available on the team's plan, as a substitute for it.
questions.explanation: With every check turned off, the only safe place is an isolated, throwaway environment where nothing important can be damaged or leaked (B). Reviewing diffs afterward doesn't prevent destructive commands or leaks at run time (A). Branch protection doesn't sandbox what commands can do (C). Auto mode still screens actions, while bypassPermissions screens nothing, so one doesn't replace the other (D).

questions.stem: A team defines a reviewer subagent with permissionMode set to plan, intending it to be read-only. The main Claude Code session is running in bypassPermissions mode. What happens when the reviewer runs?
options: The reviewer stays read-only, because a subagent's own permissionMode takes priority over the session's mode.
The reviewer inherits bypassPermissions; to keep it read-only, restrict it with a tools allowlist.
The reviewer fails to start, because its permission mode conflicts with the main session's current mode.
The main session switches to plan mode for as long as the reviewer subagent is running.
questions.explanation: When the main session runs in bypassPermissions, acceptEdits or auto mode, subagents run in that same mode and their own permissionMode is ignored (B); a subagent's own permissionMode doesn't take priority here (A). To make a subagent truly read-only, limit which tools it has at all, for example tools: Read, Grep, Glob. There is no conflict error (C), and the main session's mode doesn't change (D).

questions.stem: A reviewer subagent is defined with disallowedTools: Write, Edit. During a run, it still modified a configuration file. What is the most likely explanation?
options: It still had the Bash tool and changed the file with a shell command such as sed -i.
