disallowedTools only applies to the main session and is ignored by subagents.
Subagents ignore their definition file whenever they are started in the background by the main session.
The Edit tool is turned back on automatically after the first denied attempt.
questions.explanation: Blocking Write and Edit doesn't block file changes made through the shell. With Bash available, commands like sed -i or echo > file still modify files (A). For a truly read-only reviewer, also remove Bash or restrict it with deny rules. disallowedTools does apply to subagents (B), definitions are respected in the background (C), and denied tools don't switch themselves back on (D).

questions.stem: An engineer running a Claude Code agent team asks one teammate to create its own sub-team of three teammates for a smaller part of the problem. What happens?
options: It works: teammates can create their own teammates, up to three levels below the lead.
It isn't allowed: only the lead creates teammates, though a teammate can still use subagents.
It works, but the new teammates replace the original lead as coordinators of the team.
It isn't allowed, because an agent team is limited to three teammates in total, and the lead has already used that limit.
questions.explanation: Agent teams can't be nested: only the lead creates and shuts down teammates, and there is one team per session (B). A teammate that needs help with a sub-problem can delegate to subagents instead. The three-levels rule applies to subagents spawning subagents, not to teams (A). Leadership can't change hands (C), and there is no hard limit of three teammates, although 3 to 5 is the recommended size (D).

questions.stem: Developers on a team keep typing the same multi-step instructions to have Claude Code write release notes from recent commits. What is the best way to share this workflow?
options: Post the instructions on the team wiki, and ask developers to copy and paste them into Claude Code whenever they need them.
Add a project skill or custom slash command in the repository's .claude folder that everyone can run.
Ask each developer to save the instructions in their own personal settings file.
Add the full instructions to the beginning of every file in the repository.
questions.explanation: Workflows checked into the repo's .claude folder, as a skill or custom slash command, are shared, versioned with the code, and run the same way for everyone (B). Copying from a wiki is manual and drifts (A). Personal settings aren't shared (C). Instructions in every file clutter the code and context (D).

questions.stem: A repository's CLAUDE.md has grown to 2,000 lines, including full API references and old meeting notes. Claude Code now misses some important rules in it. What should the team do?
options: Add a line at the top saying that every rule in the file is important.
Keep CLAUDE.md short with key commands and rules, and move long references into separate files it points to with @imports.
Repeat the most important rules several times throughout the 2,000 lines.
Delete CLAUDE.md and rely on Claude Code exploring the codebase, which shows it the conventions as they actually are.
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session, so it should be short and focused. Long reference material can live in separate files linked with @path imports, or simply be read when needed (B). A note saying everything is important doesn't help (A). Repeating rules adds to the bloat (C). Deleting it loses the key rules (D).

questions.stem: A developer wants three Claude Code sessions working in parallel on separate features in the same repository, without the sessions overwriting each other's files. What is the standard approach?
options: Run all three sessions in the same folder, and ask each session to edit different files.
Use separate git worktrees, so each session works in its own folder on its own branch.
Run the sessions one after another rather than at the same time, so they can't interfere with each other.
Copy the repository three times by hand, and merge the copies back later without using git.
questions.explanation: Git worktrees give each session its own working folder and branch from the same repository, so parallel sessions can't step on each other's files (B). Sharing one folder invites conflicts (A). Running in sequence loses the parallelism (C). Manual copies outside git make merging painful (D).

questions.stem: A team wants developers to be able to write '@claude fix the failing test' in a pull request comment and have Claude Code make the change on that branch. What should they set up?
options: A chat bot that copies the PR comment into a developer's local terminal session.
The Claude Code GitHub Action in the repository, triggered by mentions in issues and pull requests.
A nightly script that reads all new PR comments, runs Claude Code on each one, and replies to them the next morning.
A rule in CLAUDE.md telling Claude Code to watch GitHub for new comments.
questions.explanation: The Claude Code GitHub Action responds to @claude mentions in issues and PRs and can make commits on the branch, within the permissions you configure (B). Copying comments into a local terminal (A) or a nightly script (C) isn't the same workflow. CLAUDE.md can't make Claude Code watch GitHub (D).

questions.stem: A CI script runs Claude Code in headless mode and then tries to read the result with a regular expression that keeps breaking on different wording. What is the better approach?
options: Ask Claude Code in the prompt to reply using exactly the same sentence format every time, so the regex keeps matching.
Use the JSON output format option, and read the result fields from the JSON.
Save the output to a file and have a person read it after each CI run, then record the result by hand.
Run the same command twice and keep whichever output the regex can parse.
questions.explanation: Headless mode can output JSON, which gives structured fields such as the result and cost that scripts can parse reliably (B). Asking for fixed wording is fragile (A). Manual reading defeats CI automation (C). Running twice doubles the cost and still may not parse (D).

questions.stem: A platform lead is choosing Claude Code permission modes for different situations. Match each situation to the most suitable mode.
choices: plan
acceptEdits
dontAsk
bypassPermissions
rows: A developer wants Claude to explore an unfamiliar codebase and propose an approach before any file is changed.
A locked-down CI job should run only the tools pre-approved in its settings, and anything else should be refused without a prompt.
A developer is iterating on code they are reviewing in their editor and wants file edits applied without approving each one.
questions.explanation: Row 1: plan mode lets Claude read and propose without editing source code (A). Row 2: dontAsk runs only pre-approved tools and doesn't prompt, which suits locked-down CI (C). Row 3: acceptEdits applies file edits automatically while the developer reviews them (B). bypassPermissions (D) approves everything and is meant only for isolated containers and VMs, so it fits none of these.

questions.stem: A team's Claude Code sessions keep making the same mistakes: they run the full test suite instead of the affected package's tests, and they forget the repository's migration naming convention. Each engineer has been correcting Claude by hand in every session. Which change makes the fix stick for the whole team?
options: Ask each engineer to remind Claude at the start of every session, using a shared snippet kept in the team wiki.
Add the test command and migration convention to the project's CLAUDE.md, committed to the repository, and keep it short and specific.
Write the conventions into each engineer's personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md file, so the reminders follow the engineers across all their projects.
Create a new subagent for testing and another for migrations, and ask engineers to delegate those tasks to them manually.
questions.explanation: Project conventions belong in the committed project CLAUDE.md, which every session in the repository loads, so one change fixes it for everyone (B). A wiki snippet (A) depends on each engineer remembering. Personal files (C) aren't shared and would leak these rules into unrelated projects. Subagents (D) add structure without teaching the main session the conventions.

questions.stem: An engineering manager asks who is accountable when a Claude Code session writes code that later causes a production incident. The team's current process lets engineers merge AI-written changes that pass CI without further review. Which policy best answers the question?
options: The engineer who submits or merges the change owns it, as with any code; AI-written changes get the same review and tests, plus more in high-risk areas.
Anthropic is accountable for the code that Claude writes, so incidents caused by AI-written code should be raised with the vendor through a support ticket and tracked there.
Nobody is individually accountable for AI-written code, so the team should rely on CI to catch problems and treat incidents as process failures.
The reviewer is accountable only if they changed the code by hand, otherwise accountability stays with the CI pipeline that approved it.
questions.explanation: AI assistance doesn't change ownership: the engineer who submits or merges the change owns it, and AI-written code goes through the same review and testing, with more scrutiny where risk is high (A). Shifting accountability to the vendor (B) is wrong and leaves the team unable to act. 'Nobody' (C) and 'the pipeline' (D) leave no human owner for the decision to ship.

questions.stem: A security team is configuring Claude Code for engineers who handle payment code. For each statement about permission modes and rules, select Yes if it is accurate.
statements: Deny rules apply in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions.
Plan mode prevents Claude from reading files, so it is a safe way to stop secrets from entering the context.
A subagent's own permissionMode can be overridden when the main session runs in bypassPermissions or auto mode.
questions.explanation: Statement 1: Yes. Deny rules block in every mode, which is why they are the right tool for secret paths. Statement 2: No. Plan mode reads files and explores; it prevents edits, not reads. Statement 3: Yes. When the main session runs in bypassPermissions, acceptEdits or auto mode, subagents run in that mode, so a read-only subagent needs a restricted tool list.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude Code to run the formatter after every file edit and to block any commit that adds a file under /secrets. Today both rules are written in CLAUDE.md, and both are skipped in about one session in ten. What should the team do?
options: Rewrite both rules in CLAUDE.md in capital letters with an example, and move them to the top of the file so they are read first.
Package both rules as a Skill, so Claude loads the detailed instructions whenever it edits files or prepares a commit.
Ask engineers to check each session's output for formatting and secrets before they push, and add both rules to the team's onboarding checklist for new engineers.
Add a PostToolUse hook that runs the formatter and a PreToolUse hook that blocks commits touching /secrets, with CI as a backstop.
questions.explanation: Rules that must always happen should be enforced by hooks, which run every time, rather than by instructions the model may skip; CI provides a final gate (D). Stronger wording (A) and Skills (B) are still instructions the model can miss. Manual checks (C) move the burden back to people and will also be skipped sometimes.

questions.stem: A team lead is configuring Claude Code for a shared repository. Match each need to the right place to configure it.
choices: The project's committed CLAUDE.md
A hook in the project's committed settings
The developer's personal .claude/settings.local.json
Managed settings deployed by IT
rows: Tell every session in the repository which command runs the tests for a single package.
Run the type checker automatically after every file edit, for everyone on the team.
Block access to credential files on every developer machine in the company, without exceptions.
questions.explanation: Row 1: shared guidance such as the test command belongs in the committed project CLAUDE.md (A). Row 2: something that must happen every time, for everyone, is a hook in the committed project settings (B). Row 3: a company-wide rule that can't be overridden belongs in managed settings (D). Personal local settings (C) are for one developer's overrides and enforce nothing for the team.
